title: Mutation Testing for Multi-Agent Workflows
author: Nafiseh Kahani
Mojtaba Bagherzadeh
abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are defined by explicit workflows, agents, tools, tool-access rules, and delegation paths. Most evaluations, however, report end-to-end task success rather than whether a test suite can detect faults in this coordination structure, such as a removed delegation, a silently removed restriction, a misrouted tool edge, or a faulty tool implementation. We adapt mutation analysis to this setting, fourteen operators in four families (delegation, allowed-tool, restriction, agent/instruction) perturb a normalized workflow manifest, and three kill criteria score whether a suite catches the change, namely K-Struct on the observed coordination, KOutcome on the task verdict or step sequence, and K-Safety on a forbidden tool call. Every criterion is evaluated by executing each suite against the original and the mutant through the OpenAI Agents SDK, with k=3 repeats and a majority vote. On ten OpenAI Agents SDK-derived workflows (49 reachable agents, 47 tools, 403 obligations), the evaluation executes 29,601 agent runs over a pool of 1,084 mutants. We use T-Struct only as a full-obligation reference point (MSstrict=1.000 under all three criteria) and measure how much the baseline suites miss, the bestperforming one (T-Dev*) reaches 0.717 (K-Struct) and only 0.559 (K-Safety). Restriction-removal (RES-REM) is the least detected fault for the baselines (0.19 to 0.28 vs 1.000). Executing the suites also allows the obligation-preserving operators (TOOL-FAULT, AG-SWAP, AG-PROMPTDROP) to be evaluated. A manifest-only oracle would not witness these changes. In this setting, tasksuccess- style suites catch only about half of permission violations.

title: From Prompt Engineering to Programmatic Prompting: Toward a Software Engineering Discipline for Large Language Models
author: Sebastian Dingler
abstract: The practice of instructing large language models (LLMs) through natural-language prompts has, in the span of a few years, migrated from an interactive curiosity to a load-bearing component of production software. Yet the vocabulary, tooling, and mental models of the field remain anchored in its interactive origins: we still speak of "prompt engineering" as though the crafting of a single well-worded instruction were the central problem. This paper argues for a categorical distinction. Prompt engineering, we contend, is an interaction technique - a human-computer interaction skill for eliciting desired behavior from a model in a conversational or exploratory setting. Programmatic prompting, by contrast, is an engineering discipline governing the behavioral interface between software systems and language models: the construction, composition, versioning, testing, and maintenance of prompts as first-class software artifacts embedded in larger systems. Conflating the two has produced brittle applications, unrepeatable evaluations, and an accumulation of prompt debt. We make three contributions: (1) a definition of programmatic prompting; (2) a systematic differentiation of programmatic prompting from prompt engineering, prompt tuning, fine-tuning, and general LLM application development; and (3) an account of prompt debt that distinguishes the self-admitted debt measurable in code from the silent debt that surfaces only as incidents, and identifies its economic cause. Our thesis is simple to state and consequential to accept: prompt engineering is an interaction technique; programmatic prompting is an engineering discipline.

title: Process then Retrieve: Investigating the Origins of the Modality Gap in Vision-Language Models
author: Arpita Shanbhag
Julia Tran
Dhruv Mandala
Ayda Sultan
abstract: Understanding the origins of the modality gap in vision language models remains a significant challenge. This work investigates whether differences in information density between modality specific tokens at the embedding layer contribute to this imbalance. We show that text tokens enter the model with much lower semantic density than visual tokens, driving early layers to focus on processing text representations before combining them with vision. Through mechanistic analysis, we demonstrate that replacing vision token positions with their semantically closest text token counterparts elicits increased attention to those positions in early layers. These findings provide a foundation for addressing the modality gap and provide insight to improve multimodal reasoning in VLM architectures.

title: Generative AI and Oral Proficiency: How ChatGPT Is Transforming English Language Speaking Practice
author: Mohammad Mousazadeh
abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into language learning contexts presents potential for developing oral proficiency, though empirical evidence regarding its efficacy remains limited. This quasi-experimental study investigated the impact of ChatGPT-mediated speaking practice on English oral proficiency among Iranian learners. A total of 380 participants (190 female, 190 male; M(age) = 21.4, SD = 4.7) from Tehran and Isfahan were assigned to experimental (ChatGPT practice; n = 190) or control (human pair work; n = 190) groups. Both groups completed an 8-week intervention with three 30-minute weekly sessions. Oral proficiency was assessed using a Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR)-aligned Oral Proficiency Interview (OPI) scored on fluency, pronunciation, lexical resource, grammatical accuracy, and interactive communication (total score: 0-20). Multilevel growth modeling revealed a significant time-by-group interaction, F(1, 376) = 48.73, p < .001, partial eta-squared = .115. The experimental group demonstrated greater gains (M change = 2.90, SD = 1.60) than controls (M change = 0.75, SD = 1.80), d = 1.20, 95% CI [0.95, 1.45]. Gender moderated this effect, with females in the experimental group showing the largest improvements (M change = 2.50). Mediation analysis confirmed that increased integrative motivation partially mediated proficiency gains (indirect effect = 0.28, 95% CI [0.20, 0.36]). Findings indicate that structured ChatGPT practice yields modest but meaningful enhancements in oral proficiency, particularly when leveraging affective factors. Implications for AI-augmented speaking pedagogy in resource-constrained contexts are discussed.

title: KR A1: Design and Preliminary Evaluation of a Humanoid-Robot Interaction Prototype Integrating Personalized Voice Synthesis, Contextual Dialogue, and Emotion-Aware Response Generation
author: Mahek Aanthu
Om Aanthu
Aaryan AK Aanthu
abstract: This paper presents the design and preliminary evaluation of KR A1, a humanoid-robot interaction prototype that integrates personalized voice synthesis, contextual dialogue processing, and emotion-aware response generation for potential mental-healthcare applications. The system architecture combines a locally hosted large language model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, served via Ollama) for natural-language understanding and response generation, OpenVoice v2 for zero-shot speaker-adaptive speech synthesis, and a two-tier emotion-processing pipeline comprising a keyword heuristic and LLM-based inference. Face recognition (InsightFace) and vector memory retrieval (FAISS with sentence-transformer embeddings) enable user-personalized interaction. The experimental evaluation reported here is limited to the voice-cloning component: cloned voices were evaluated against reference recordings using eight acoustic similarity measures - mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, pitch, spectral centroid, spectral contrast, spectral rolloff, zero-crossing rate, formants, and speaker-embedding cosine similarity - supplemented by a same-speaker versus cross-speaker baseline comparison. All tests were conducted on a small, informal development sample; no statistical significance testing against a held-out baseline was performed. The emotion-recognition accuracy, end-to-end response latency, and therapeutic or clinical impact of the integrated system have not yet been formally evaluated and are identified as directions for future work. All testing was informal and self-conducted by the development team; no patients or external human participants were involved, and the system has not been evaluated or deployed in a clinical setting.

title: Beyond One User and One Model: Rethinking LLMs as Mediators in Collaborative Sensemaking and Ideation
author: Pengqi Wang
Emily Kuang
abstract: As LLMs enter qualitative data workflows, they are predominantly designed for individual researchers rather than collaborative teams, which risks disrupting the collective negotiation essential to sensemaking, driving premature consensus, and potentially erasing marginalized voices. In this position paper, we argue that LLMs must be reconceived as active team mediators. Grounded in empirical studies of human-LLM collaborative analysis, we propose three design directions: quote-level traceability to preserve accountability of human and LLM contributions, controllable delegation boundaries to maintain researcher agency across workflow stages, and structured dissent mechanisms to surface interpretive conflicts that teams might otherwise suppress. We ground these directions in accessibility research as a domain where methodological rigor and representational equity are obligatory.

title: Building Rapport with Self-Disclosure in Human-Robot Interaction
author: Haritha Anupindi
Chayan Sarkar
Tapas Nayak
Marynel Vazquez
abstract: As social robots become increasingly present in everyday environments, establishing rapport with users is critical for enabling sustained and meaningful human-robot interaction. In human-human communication, self-disclosure is a well-established mechanism for building rapport; however, its role and impact in human-robot interaction (HRI) are not yet well understood. Although recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have improved the linguistic competence of conversational robots, such systems are typically deployed as reactive information providers, offering limited social reciprocity and relational depth. In this article, we investigate the role of robot self-disclosure in fostering rapport during face-to-face human-robot interaction. We propose a dialogue system, called RADIA that leverages retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to enable a robot to retrieve and reference simulated autobiographical memories, allowing first-person self-disclosure to be incorporated naturally into ongoing conversations. We evaluate the proposed approach through an in-person user study, comparing interactions with a self-disclosing robot against a baseline non-self-disclosing robot. Our results show that robot self-disclosure significantly influences conversational dynamics and enhances users' perceived rapport with the robot, suggesting that self-disclosure is a valuable social behavior for long-term and socially engaging human-robot interaction.

title: How to start a conversation proactively?
author: Mohit Nathani
Aaditya Gupta
Eshwar Dhande
Chayan Sarkar
abstract: Proactively initiating a conversation is a fundamental social competence and a critical capability for social robots. However, determining how and when to start a conversation in a given situation remains an open challenge, primarily due to the lack of a principled definition of conversational context. While recent large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive conversational fluency, they are predominantly turn-reactive and often produce generic or monotonous openers when tasked with initiating interaction, even when contextual information is available. Such limitations are particularly problematic for embodied social robots, where inappropriate or poorly timed initiations can negatively affect user engagement and rapport. In this work, we propose a schema of contextual variables that jointly characterize situations relevant for proactive conversation initiation. The schema is designed to structure perceptual, situational, and interactional cues such that they can be effectively exploited by language models. Furthermore, motivated by the absence of suitable training data, we introduce a curated dataset of contextually-aligned conversation openers (CCO) covering diverse everyday scenarios. Using this dataset, we fine-tune small language models (SLMs) to generate proactive conversation initiations. Through a comparative evaluation involving zero-shot LLMs, off-the-shelf SLMs, and our fine-tuned models, we demonstrate that explicit contextual structuring and targeted data curation substantially improve the quality and contextual appropriateness of conversation openers. Our results highlight the importance of context modeling for proactive social interaction and provide actionable building blocks for conversational robots.

title: Cross-Modal Associations in Creativity: Evaluating Word-Image Pairing in Humans and Large Language Models
author: Eva Illion
Linxuan Wang
Liane Gabora
abstract: Given differences in the associative memory architectures of humans and AI, it is not clear whether AI generates and interprets visual-linguistic associations the way humans do. To investigate this, human participants and two large language models (LLMs), ChatGPT and Gemini, were asked to generate novel words and corresponding images that form meaningfully linked dyads. The LLMs and a second group of human participants were presented with shuffled sets of these words and images and asked to rematch them in ways they felt were most meaningful. Humans performed similarly regardless of whether the pairs were human or LLM-generated, while LLMs were better at matching LLM-generated pairs. Overall, LLMs outperformed humans at recovering the intended pairings. These findings suggest that despite architectural differences, the way in which AI generates and detects associations between language and visual stimuli is not only like that of hu-mans, but they may be superior at recognizing cross-domain associations that humans find meaningful.

title: Can You Spot the Virtual Patient (VP)? Expert Evaluation, Turing Test, Linguistic Analysis, and Semantic Similarity Analysis
author: Reyhaneh Hosseinpourkhoshkbari
Wei-chen Huang
Suvel Muttreja
Richard M. Golden
abstract: Communication is a core clinical competency and essential for safe, effective patient care. Virtual patients (VPs) powered by large language models (LLMs) offer a promising alternative to traditional formats such as standardized patients (SPs). However, few studies have quantitatively as well as qualitatively evaluated their realism across diverse clinical scenarios using behavioral studies and linguistic dialog analyses. This study evaluated the realism of GPT-4o-generated VPs through expert review, Turing testing, linguistic analysis, and semantic analysis. We generated 44 VPs using structured illness scripts derived from doctor-simulated patient dialogues across 17 clinical categories. Experts annotated responses for hallucinations, omissions, and repetitions, with high interrater reliability (ICC > 0.77). A Turing test revealed that participants struggled to distinguish VP responses from those of real patients, with average classification accuracy for VP responses falling below chance level. Lexical and syntactic analyses of over 2,000 conversation turns showed that VP responses were generally realistic, more formal and lexically consistent, while human responses displayed greater emotional variation. Semantic similarity using BioClinicalBERT and cosine similarity averaged 0.871 at the response level and 0.842 at the transcript level. Our findings support the integration of LLM-based VPs in communication training while highlighting areas for trust, transparency, and refinement, contributing to both GenAI deployment in healthcare and its safety evaluation.

title: Micro-Randomized Trial of an AI-Simulated Practice Tool for Therapeutic Skills
author: Ryan Louie
Ellen Converse
Diyi Yang
Emma Brunskill
abstract: Though LLM-simulated practice may support psychotherapy education, open questions remain about which system features provide the most educational value. We developed an AI-simulated practice tool for use in psychotherapy classrooms that provides speaking practice with LLM-based patients, followed by a post-practice activity that includes feedback from a fine-tuned LLM and written reflection exercises. We deployed the tool in a graduate psychotherapy course (n=25, 5 weeks) using a micro-randomized trial (MRT) - a method which can estimate the causal excursion effect of an intervention by leveraging longitudinal repeated randomization with participants. Testing four conditions crossing AI feedback (present/absent) with reflection granularity (utterance/session-level), we found surprising interaction effects on student engagement and educational value: utterance-level reflection paired with AI feedback significantly outperformed all conditions. Students valued comparing the AI suggestions to their own rather than passively accepting them. As the first MRT in a health education setting testing an LLM-simulation system, this work demonstrates that MRTs, a method mostly used in mobile intervention research, offers a viable evaluation paradigm for AI systems deployed in health education settings.

title: Engagement Estimation in Human-Robot and Human-Human Interactions across Domain, Age and Culture: MultiMediate'26 Challenge
author: Marius Funk
Daksitha Withanage Don
Michal Balazia
Victor Oei
Shogo Okada
FranÃ§ois BrÃ©mond
Andreas Bulling
Elisabeth AndrÃ©
Philipp MÃ¼ller
abstract: Understanding engagement in human interaction is essential for modelling assistive and context-aware AI systems. Previously, the MultiMediate challenge has focused on estimating momentary continuous engagement values in adult conversation across cultures, achieving high levels of generalisability across domains. However, engagement can be measured in different metrics and manifest differently between children and adults. MultiMediate'26 therefore expands the evaluated domain set to include the PInSoRo dataset of Child-Child and Child-Robot play sessions in English. These sessions were annotated categorically with task and social engagement, diversifying engagement types, age ranges and interaction types. In this paper, we describe the MultiMediate'26 challenge and its goals, introduce the NoXi, NoXi-J, MPIIGI, and PInSoRo datasets, showcase extracted multi-modal features, present our baseline model for engagement estimation across all domains, and discuss challenge submissions and approaches. In an effort to provide a transparent and welcoming challenge environment, baseline code, leaderboard, datasets, and extracted features are publicly available at https://github.com/hcmlab/MultiMediate_26.

title: Industry case studies of adapting TTS for smooth interactions
author: Paige TuttÃ¶si
ElÃ©onore Ferrier-Barbut
Anais Scipioni
Olivia Yung
Ha Eun Shim
Ajla Basic
Yue Wang
H. Henny Yeung
abstract: Modern, neural-based ASR and TTS systems for speech communication are now very sophisticated, but they are frequently designed for average users in more idealized scenarios, which can underperform when interacting with users having specialized listening needs, or who speak in non-standard ways. Here we review recent TTS research, and note that industrial, production-level implementations of adaptive TTS systems are scarce. We describe how we implemented changes to TTS systems based on prior research, and then report qualitative results from two case studies, where adapted TTS techniques are applied to real-world HRI settings: First, in an older adult care home, and second, in an airport, where noise levels create comprehension problems. Results suggest promising directions using relatively simple modifications to pitch, duration, and intensity of the robot's speech, and offer a framework for larger, more formal studies of how TTS adaptations can improve HRI.

title: Semantic-Enhanced Sparse Temporal Modeling for Dynamic Engagement Estimation in Multimodal Interactions
author: Yangchen Yu
Taoliang Wang
Jia Li
Nor Mazlina Ghazali
Mohd Nazim Mohtar
Bingkun Bao
Richang Hong
abstract: Dynamic engagement estimation aims to infer participants' evolving engagement states from continuous multimodal interaction streams. Existing approaches typically combine acoustic, pose, and visual representations with temporal models to capture observable interaction patterns. However, conversational semantics are difficult to align with frame-level engagement annotations in the same manner as continuous audio-visual signals, leaving dialogue context less effectively exploited in existing temporal modeling pipelines. Moreover, engagement annotations often evolve smoothly over time, making dense frame-level modeling computationally redundant and potentially sensitive to local annotation noise. To address these issues, we propose SEST, a Semantically-Enhanced Sparse Temporal framework that models engagement-related information from both semantic and temporal perspectives. SEST leverages Multimodal Large Language Models to extract multimodal semantic embeddings, providing dialogue-aware contextual information beyond conventional frame-level features. In parallel, SEST replaces dense-to-dense temporal modeling with a sparse-to-dense pathway, where continuous frame sequences are first encoded into compact temporal dynamics to reduce redundant computation and broaden temporal coverage, then fused with semantic context and recovered to the original label resolution for dense engagement prediction. Experiments on the MEE2026 benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of SEST, which achieved first place in the challenge.

title: Personalized Alignment of Language Models with Human Value Profiles
author: Rashon Poole
Farnaz Jahanbakhsh
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for subjective tasks such as seeking advice, where there is often no single correct answer. Yet dominant alignment methods learn a single behavior policy that applies uniformly across users, limiting their ability to reflect individual value priorities. We propose personalized value alignment, a framework for adapting model responses to users' stable value profiles rather than to personas, demographics, or task-specific preferences used in prior personalization work. Our approach represents users through Schwartz value profiles and selects which of their values are relevant to each query before applying targeted prompting, activation steering, or LoRA-DPO. We create a dataset of 1,501 value-tension scenarios and evaluate over 152 diverse value profiles sampled from a nationally representative survey. Value-targeted methods outperform no-personalization, demographic, and full-profile prompting baselines, indicating that gains come from focused conditioning on query-specific value priorities rather than mere exposure. We further find that steering effects are not uniform across users: alignment gains vary by where a user's priorities fall in the value space. Combining targeted prompting with activation steering or LoRA-DPO yields the strongest personalization while keeping logical quality within adequate range.

title: Grounding Insight: An Artificial Affect Signal for Human-Centric Explainability of RL Agents
author: Bernhard Hilpert
Kim Baraka
Joost Broekens
abstract: In Human-Interactive Robot Learning (HIRL), human teachers assess learning progress by observing agent behavior. However, Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents often fail to express learning progress in human-interpretable ways, leading to suboptimal or counterproductive teaching. This work proposes "Insight": a human-interpretable affective signal grounded in the RL process. It is specifically designed to address the "Absence of learning" human teacher mental model misalignment - the misconception that a failing or exploring agent is broken, underpowered or not learning at all - by signaling an agent's "Aha!" Insight moment. The signal is derived from the absolute Temporal Difference (TD) error making it easily implementable in other RL agents. To ground this signal, five design criteria were formulated: Relevance, Interpretability, Faithfulness, Scalability, Generalizability. The structural construct validity was assessed through simulation, examining micro and macro dynamics and event-related sensitivity. Micro dynamics reveal that Insight captures meaningful learning events at the appropriate time and magnitude. Macro dynamics demonstrate that the signal follows the agent's learning phases and reflects overall progress. Event-related sensitivity shows, the signal distinguishes the saliency of environment interactions, such as positive rewards versus "trauma-like" negative events. These results demonstrate that technical RL dynamics can be effectively packaged into human-like affective substrates to close the teacher-learner loop.

title: Autonomy Is Absent, Not Eroded: An Observational Study of User Autonomy in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations
author: Chaoran Chen
Isabel BarberÃ¡
Yuhuai Wei
abstract: Does prolonged interaction with Large Language Models reduce users' observable autonomy during conversation? We test this degradation hypothesis by scoring user autonomy across 2,877 multi-turn conversations (46,952 turns) from WildChat and validating on 500 conversations from LMSYS-Chat-1M. Our core finding is a null result: population-level autonomy remains stable throughout conversations, only 4.7% of conversations show meaningful decline, and an apparent decrease at later turn positions is explained by survivorship bias. Instead, the dominant pattern is not erosion but absence: 80.8% of conversations exhibit zero or low autonomy throughout. When autonomy engagement occurs, it is self-reinforcing (persistence doubles from 40% to 85% over consecutive turns). These findings reframe the problem: the risk is not that LLMs progressively degrade users' observable autonomy, but that most users never engage in independent reasoning during the interaction.

title: Preference-Augmented Distributional Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Sensitive Navigation
author: Zhaofan Zhang
Yue Chang
Rufeng Chen
Hechang Chen
Sihong Xie
Hui Xiong
abstract: Ensuring safe and reliable navigation under diverse sources of uncertainty remains a central challenge for autonomous systems. Within distributional reinforcement learning (DistRL), Implicit Quantile Networks (IQN) have attracted interest for navigation under uncertainty because they enable risk adaptation through flexible quantile sampling. Existing approaches, however, typically use a fixed or randomly sampled Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) level during training and adjust the risk level during deployment using hand-tuned hyperparameters or external sensor signals. This scalar-CVaR formulation confines learning to a narrow family of tail-risk preferences, creating a mismatch between training-time preference exposure and deployment-time risk adjustment. We instead represent variations in risk preference as shifts in quantile-weight distributions and expose the agent to diverse preferences through preference-guided exploration. At deployment, we optimize against the worst-case preference distribution to derive a conservative policy that accounts for multiple risk profiles. This reduces hyperparameter tuning and reliance on limited sensor signals under partial observability. Experiments across simulated environments and vehicle platforms show that our method reduces collisions while improving task success.

title: BIBIMBAP: A Benchmark for Instructional BIM-Based Automated Programming
author: Clemens Kujat
Bharathi Kannan Nithyanantham
Stefan Telgmann
Tobias Sesterhenn
Joern Ploennigs
Stefan LÃ¼dtke
Christian Bartelt
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are emerging as natural-language interfaces for Building Information Modeling (BIM), successfully achieving information retrieval, but no benchmark exists to evaluate their ability to edit Industry Foundation Classes (IFC). We introduce BIBIMBAP, a Text-to-BIM benchmark with 100 curated tasks covering Create-Read-Update-Delete (CRUD) operations across spatial, geometric, topological, numeric, and conceptual categories. Each task includes a natural-language prompt, an IFC model, expected structured outputs, and test scripts for automated evaluation. Baseline results show limited performance (best: 50.2%) and frequent failures in constraint preservation and spatial reasoning, with some correct outputs achieved despite flawed reasoning.

title: Causal Discovery Bench: Can LLMs Autonomously Conduct Effective Experiments?
author: Zhuoyang Liu
Ning Peng
Ming Shen
Zijun Gao
abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents get actively adopted for autonomous research, they must not only reason over existing evidence, but also design informative experiments, allocate resources, analyze sequential observations, and decide when to stop and make conclusions. Yet these capabilities remain poorly measured. We introduce Causal-Discovery-Bench (https://github.com/mshen1019/causal-discovery-bench), a verifiable sandbox with configurable structural equation models and resource constraints to evaluate sequential experimental design and causal discovery without domain-semantic cues. Across 3,802 episodes with 13 models from 5 vendors, we analyze agent behavior along 40 metrics in seven families. Agents' performance exhibits a four-level difficulty hierarchy spanning single-experiment design, sequential exploration of causal relationships, resource-aware experimentation balancing cost and statistical power, and autonomous resolution of conflicting evidence. We identify a substantial performance gap between causal inference from correctly curated evidence and navigating causal discovery through autonomous experimentation: Analyzing agents' action trajectories attributes 94.5% of their mistakes to experimental design rather than to inference, which is further consolidated with ablation studies. Relaxing resource constraints alone does not reliably resolve failures in sequential discovery. In contrast, basic statistical tools substantially improve performance across multiple model families, while advanced tools provide little additional benefit when models lack prerequisite lower-level capabilities.

title: How Many Examples, and Which Ones? A Study of In-Context Learning for Natural Language Inference
author: Georgos Dikaios
Isidoros Perikos
Ioannis Hatzilygeroudis
abstract: Natural language inference (NLI) is a fundamental task of natural language processing and crucial for evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of AI methods. Research has mostly focused on encoder or encoder-decoder architectures. However, the field of decoder-only Large Language Models (LLMs) remains underexplored. While prior work has mainly investigated complex sampling and prompting techniques, the effectiveness of a minimalistic prompting approach is yet to be examined in decoder-only LLMs. In this work, we examine and provide a comprehensive benchmark of LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and Phi 4) in this domain, across the MNLI, QNLI and SciTail datasets. The performance of these models was evaluated using zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies with simple and direct prompts. The results of the article indicate that LLMs generally perform exceptionally well when they are provided with a simple, straightforward prompt, challenging the notion that complex prompting techniques are always required for NLI tasks. Additionally, we find that the choice of demonstration label in one-shot prompting significantly affects performance for most models, with entailment-primed examples performing best. Our findings also show that the use of a few representative examples, in the case of few-shot, produced performance comparable or superior to prompts with higher example counts, although the efficacy of the prompting techniques is model and dataset-dependent. Moreover, our simple prompting approach consistently matched or outperformed more elaborate methods such as ICS and MCQ-based prompting.

title: Efficient Learning of Differentiable MPC Policies on the GPU via Smoothed ADMM and First-Order Reinforcement Learning
author: Jianghan Zhang
Roland Schwan
Gabriel Bravo-Palacios
John Zhang
Thomas Lew
Brian Plancher
abstract: Differentiable model predictive control (MPC) enables structured, constraint-aware policies to be optimized end-to-end. However, learning MPC policies faces two bottlenecks: (1) nonsmooth sensitivities at active-set transitions and (2) expensive policy evaluation, since each requires an optimization solve. We first introduce SmoothedTurboMPC, a GPU-parallel differentiable MPC solver combining sequential quadratic programming (SQP) with a log-barrier-smoothed alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) inner solver. Its design enables smooth gradients, exact sensitivities at convergence, and efficient execution on GPUs. Second, to efficiently train MPC policies, we pair our solver with first-order reinforcement learning (FORL) using Short-Horizon Actor-Critic (SHAC), which reuses rollout MPC solutions instead of repeatedly re-evaluating them. Comparisons with state of the art solvers show that the approach achieves up to $4.4\times$ higher end-to-end training throughput. On a vehicle racing task, our method achieves higher returns than MPC PPO with a $46\times$ speedup, training on 3.3 million transitions in only 7 minutes. Finally, we use the framework to train a more reliable MPC racing policy via RL with domain randomization, and validate it on a full-scale race car. We integrate our advances into the open-source TurboMPC solver.

title: DramaGrow: A Regime-Aware Benchmark for Auditing LLM Judges of Multi-Episode Drama
author: Hui Zhang
Yibo Su
abstract: LLMs can now draft complete multi-episode dramas, and LLM judges are increasingly used to evaluate them. Assessing the reliability of these judges is difficult because drama quality encompasses specification-backed errors, reproducible preferences, and legitimate disagreement among human raters. Most existing evaluations reduce these cases to a single score from one judge call and leave tie calibration, call-to-call variation, and the vote margin underlying the human reference unreported. We introduce DramaGrow, a regime-aware benchmark and audit protocol for AI-generated Chinese five-episode drama. The benchmark assigns verifiable constraint violations, four-of-five preferences, and within-panel disagreements to separate denominators and evidence rules. It contains 800 episodes, 120 byte-preserving interventions, and 1,155 blinded five-rater records, including a frozen extension with 114 supermajority pairs and 21 disagreement pairs. On the frozen sets of 114 preference pairs and 35 constraint interventions, the repeated absolute-score rubrics yield overlapping performance, with mean accuracies of 53.8-55.8% and three-call agreement of 29.8-32.5%, and their accuracy falls from 71.6-71.9% to 34.8-37.1% as the tie band widens. DirectPair-GLM reaches 85.1% preference accuracy, 89.5% constraint F1, and 81.9% Detect+Locate on the same items, and exact subpanel enumeration identifies four-of-five as the smallest stable human vote margin. Evaluation protocol, tie calibration, judge-call variation, and panel margin therefore affect performance as much as rubric design. We will release the specification packages, scripts, interventions, anonymized human votes and rationales, frozen judge runs, and analysis code.

title: Rethinking Supervision Targets for Multimodal LLM Unlearning: Less Private Information, Reduced Distribution Shift
author: Leijiang Gu
Zhen Zeng
Feng Li
Le Zhang
Zenglin Shi
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can memorize and reproduce sensitive information from their training data, posing significant privacy risks. Their ability to encode knowledge across both textual and visual modalities further complicates the selective removal of such private information. Many existing methods guide model unlearning by training the model toward constructed labels or output distributions, which we refer to as supervision targets. However, these methods often suffer from a trade-off between forgetting effectiveness and model utility. We identify supervision target limitations as a key factor in this trade-off and empirically show that targets containing more private information lead to insufficient forgetting, while larger distribution shifts from the original output distribution are associated with greater utility degradation. Motivated by these findings, we propose FFN-Perturbed Self-Distillation (FPD), which starts from the teacher's original output distribution as a zero-shift reference and selectively perturbs FFN activations associated with private information across textual and visual modalities. By precisely reducing private information from the teacher's original output distribution, FPD constructs supervision targets with less private information and reduced distribution shift. Extensive experiments on S-MLLMUn Bench demonstrate that FPD achieves a better forgetting-utility trade-off than existing methods.

title: A Model Organism for Studying Unverbalized Evaluation Awareness
author: Daniel Donnelly
Evan Chapple
Haritz Puerto
Sahar Abdelnabi
abstract: Large language models can recognize when they are being evaluated and change their behavior accordingly, undermining the reliability of safety benchmarks. Evaluation awareness (EA) is usually measured by having an LLM judge scan reasoning traces for explicit statements of recognition, but this signal is increasingly unreliable. Recent frontier-model system cards report a drop in verbalized rates between releases, which is indistinguishable from awareness that has gone unverbalized. Interpretability methods could detect such unverbalized evaluation awareness (UEA) in individual interactions, but lack instance-level ground truth. Asking the model alters the input, and dataset labels do not reveal whether it recognized a particular prompt as an evaluation. We address this gap with a model organism. Using synthetic document fine-tuning, SFT, and DPO, we train Qwen3.5-27B to emit a marker (a designated token) in its final response when it recognizes an evaluation, while suppressing the marker and verbalized awareness in its reasoning. The marker largely tracks the evaluation concept as it can be strongly modulated by evaluation framing in the system prompt. When not told whether it is being evaluated, the organism recognizes evaluations from test-question cues, mirroring what its base model often verbalizes. Using the marker as a label, we benchmark linear probes, the Jacobian Lens, and Activation Oracles, built on the base model and blind to the marker. None recovers the label reliably. These results suggest that current interpretability methods are not yet reliable UEA detectors, even when recognition relies on simple cues. Our model organism offers a testbed for improving them.

title: Counting Events, Not Seeing Them: Diagnosing and Repairing the Readout Failure in Video LLMs
author: Dongwu Qian
abstract: Video LLMs fail conspicuously at counting how many times an object crosses the screen, a failure attributed to missing object permanence. Using construction-grounded synthetic testbeds with independently validated labels, we show this attribution is incomplete: the count signal is present but unread - linear probes decode per-window presence at 93% while global count decoding collapses to a duration confound. Concurrent work reports the same representation-output dissociation for repetition counting; we show that in exit-and-reappear event counting it is repairable: two readout-directed repairs (episode-localization supervision and a discrete event-symbol side channel) raise same-object counting from 46.7% to 65.0% (oracle 66.7%) on a chance-33% benchmark across 7B-30B systems. Transfer to an independent factory costs nothing, and an audit of the measurement apparatus exposes four data-integrity failures that had obscured the boundary. A real-video audit (REALCOUNT, n=18, blind-audited) shows the boundary persists - best 55.6% at chance 33.3% - and symbol transfer fails zero-shot. A 1-epoch in-domain adaptation bench is negative (six levers at 28-50%), but a 3-epoch schedule shows this is budget-limited for the symbol channel: with a 3-epoch schedule and sequence-disjoint oracle timelines the reader reaches 94.4% on REALCOUNT, and with the deployed detector's timelines a 2-epoch run reaches 72.2%. The residual gap is detector evidence and the reader's match to detector noise, not reader capacity: a frozen-feature boundary probe finds the signal weak (AUC 0.62 over a 0.51 permutation control) and non-transferring across clips (0.77 within-clip vs. 0.62 across windows).

title: Video-DCI: How Far Are VLM Agents from Human Viewers in Direct Video Corpus Interaction?
author: Garry Yang
Yuqiao Liu
Hao Lin
Luohao Pan
Xinru Chen
Wanqi Ren
Zhikang Xu
Yizhan Huang
Huaixiao Tou
James Cheng
abstract: Humans answer complex visual questions by inspecting short moments, updating what they know, and redirecting attention toward missing evidence. Existing video benchmarks, however, often provide the relevant video, evaluate only final answers or isolated localization, or permit textual shortcuts, leaving multi-round visual evidence seeking underexplored. We introduce Video-DCI, a diagnostic benchmark and functionally matched human-agent protocol for Direct Video-Corpus Interaction. It comprises DCI-Loc for temporal evidence localization and DCI-QA for end-to-end discovery, retention, and composition of cross-video evidence. In DCI-QA, videos within each pool are topically related, yet every answer requires hidden temporal evidence from multiple videos. Given only the question and video pool, humans and agents iteratively inspect bounded local windows, retain supporting evidence, and answer with cited temporal spans. Human trajectories provide reference curves for evidence acquisition and use across rounds. Experiments reveal a consistent retrieval-to-grounding gap. On DCI-Loc, frontier VLMs often retrieve and expose the reference moment, yet convert far less of this exposure into precise final citations than the human reference. On DCI-QA, the loss begins earlier and compounds across videos. Ablation studies further confirm that iterative search outperforms one-shot retrieval. Multi-round search is therefore necessary but insufficient: current agents accumulate candidates and observations more readily than precise, jointly sufficient evidence.

title: HALMES: Knowing When to Intervene in LVLM Hallucination Mitigation
author: Ruining Hu
Jiaqi Lu
Xiao Liu
Ying Shen
Yu Wang
Lin Zhang
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in multimodal tasks. Nevertheless, their outputs remain prone to object hallucinations that are inconsistent with visual content. Contrastive decoding, as a training-free inference-time mitigation approach, typically intervenes in the output distribution at every decoding step. However, such indiscriminate full-stage intervention may disrupt originally correct generations and even induce new hallucinations. To address this issue, we first analyze the relationship between internal attention features and hallucinated token segments in LVLMs, revealing that hallucination-related abnormalities already emerge progressively in preceding token segments. Based on this observation, we propose HALMES, a lightweight plug-and-play module that identifies hallucination precursor segments from attention features during generation and selectively triggers contrastive decoding. HALMES can be integrated with various full-stage contrastive decoding methods, transforming indiscriminate intervention into on-demand targeted correction. Extensive experiments across different LVLM architectures and multiple benchmarks show that HALMES further improves the hallucination mitigation performance of existing contrastive decoding methods while reducing the negative impact of full-stage intervention on normal outputs, validating the importance of modeling and selectively intervening on hallucination-prone segments.

title: A four-view smartphone video dataset of a robot-held flexible strip, with camera poses and a 3D LaGSplat baseline
author: Louen Pottier
abstract: This note describes a multi-view video dataset of a deformable object driven by a measured input, with the measured pose of every camera, and a first 3D result obtained on it with LaGSplat. LaGSplat learns from video a low-dimensional latent state that is both the generalized coordinate of a learned dissipative Lagrangian and the conditioning variable of a Gaussian Splatting decoder; fitting the decoder in 3D calls for synchronized multi-view footage, which the original paper only had from synthetic renderings. Here a robot arm moves a flexible strip by oscillating along a one-dimensional path, and four iPhones, three fixed and one handheld, film it for ten minutes. The videos are synchronized, the cameras are posed from the scene, and the position of the gripper is given per frame as the input of the system. LaGSplat fitted on this data with the gripper acceleration as a forcing term renders held-out views at 26 to 33 dB PSNR and runs as a real-time interactive demo in a web browser. Dataset, checkpoints and training code are public.

title: SceneShifter: Training-free Multi-Scene Temporal Control for Audio-driven Human Animation
author: Jianzhi Long
Rong-Cheng Tu
Hao Guan
Siyuan Liang
Shunyu Liu
Xiao Luo
Dacheng Tao
abstract: Although audio-driven human animation has achieved impressive realism, it still lacks effective Multi-Scene Temporal Control: orchestrating background transitions at precise timestamps while preserving a coherent foreground subject. We show that this challenge stems from the diffusion transformer's self-attention mechanism, and addressing it requires two capabilities: (1) Semantic-Aware Temporal Decoupling, which isolates background attention across scenes while retaining cross-scene foreground attention for subject consistency; and (2) Foreground Motion Localization, which accurately tracks the foreground subject across latent frames, especially under large motion. To address these challenges, we introduce SceneShifter, a training-free framework for precise multi-scene control in audio-driven human animation. SceneShifter guides spatio-temporal self-attention by suppressing cross-scene attention among background tokens while preserving cross-scene attention among foreground tokens. To support this guidance under large motion, SceneShifter extracts dynamic foreground masks from the self-attention layers and heads that best capture subject trajectories. We further introduce SceneShifterBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate scene-timing accuracy, foreground preservation, and visual quality under large motion, multiple subjects. Experiments show that SceneShifter achieves frame-level scene timing, strong subject preservation, and high visual quality, outperforming existing baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/JamesLong199/SceneShifter.

title: How Many Demonstrations Does a VLA Need? On the Sample Efficiency of VLA Finetuning
author: Rahul Chand
Miguel Villa Floran
abstract: Pretrained vision language action (VLA) models show strong zero-shot performance, but are rarely deployed directly and are often first post-trained on demonstrations from the target setting. Yet VLAs are typically compared by zero-shot or full-data fine-tuned success, revealing little about the data and compute required for adaptation. We study adaptation efficiency for six VLAs ($\pi_{0}$, $\pi_{0.5}$, and GR00T N1-N1.7) on four LIBERO suites, varying both demonstrations and training steps. This reveals differences hidden by full-data fine-tuning: models within two points on the full LIBERO-Spatial dataset differ by up to $3\times$ in success with 50 demonstrations. $\pi_{0.5}$ needs $2$--$5\times$ fewer demonstrations than $\pi_{0}$ and is the most sample-efficient model at every budget, with the largest gap on the long-horizon suite. Within GR00T, N1.5 adapts more efficiently than N1.6 and N1.7 on three of four suites, despite their stronger zero-shot performance. We study one pretraining factor behind these differences by freezing the VLM during finetuning: this severely degrades the $\pi$ models, whose VLM is jointly trained with the action expert during pretraining, but barely affects GR00T models. Finally, validation loss on held-out demonstrations tracks closed-loop success within a suite, but understates how much more sample-efficient $\pi_{0.5}$ is than $\pi_{0}$.

title: ReelCache: An Efficient KV Cache Compression and Management System for Multi-Round Video Generation
author: Tianyu Wang
Daiyang Yu
Zhiwei Ren
Junbo Li
Jitian Zhang
Longfei Shangguan
abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models produce large KV caches during multi-round video generation. Keeping all these KV chunks would consume substantial memory, while rebuilding discarded caches would significantly delay video chunk generation. This paper presents ReelCache, a KV cache compression system for efficient multi-round, long video generation. ReelCache combines an intra-chunk compressor with an inter-chunk cache manager. The compressor applies low-rank decomposition across channels and video coding to the resulting coefficients, predicting the decomposition rank per transformer layer online to meet retained-energy targets. The cache manager shares basis directions across consecutive chunks and organizes chunk states in a tree, allowing generation branches to share historical state while supporting restoration for resume, rewind, and fork. Experiments across five video generation models show that ReelCache reduces KV storage by 14.46-21.13x relative to baselines and accelerates next-chunk generation by 1.25-3.36x, with less than 1% drop in six representative VBench metrics. GitHub: https://github.com/Tianyu9748/ReelCache

title: Seeing Like a Shopper: Validating Vision-Language Models as Synthetic Consumers
author: Woongki Kim
Seungkook Baek
Minhyeok Lee
abstract: Language models are widely used as synthetic respondents in surveys, behavioral experiments, and market research. Most of these respondents read text, whereas shoppers in a store choose by looking at shelves, which makes vision-language models (VLMs) natural synthetic shoppers. We test whether VLM shoppers follow real consumers at two levels. At the purchase level, VLM shoppers built from household records plan their trips from a store directory and select products from shelf images, and we compare their purchases with six public datasets from three countries. The synthetic baskets hit held-out purchases as often as the households' own past trips, and synthetic group differences correlate with real ones twice as strongly as those of a trained regression. Without fitting, VLM shoppers reproduce alcohol purchases by gender and age in Russia and trip sizes by store distance in Taiwan, and respond to situations, prices, and displays within measured ranges. At the level of a single shelf choice, a model's answer confounds the product with its position and letter label. We therefore introduce ShelfSight, shelf renderings that vary products, positions, labels, viewpoints, and prices independently, together with a factor model that separates product preferences from the effects of label and position, which we call answer effects. On ShelfSight, hosted VLMs read the shelf, follow stated needs, keep their product preferences across views, and respond to price as budget shoppers. These answer effects, a preference for the letter A and for positions in the image, are estimated once per image type and removed. VLMs are thus good synthetic shoppers whose corrected shelf choices reflect product preferences.

title: Preconditioned Implicit Midpoint Langevin Sampling for Non-Smooth Bayesian Imaging
author: Sichen Wang
Zhipeng Lu
abstract: We introduce P-IMLA, a preconditioned implicit-midpoint Langevin sampler for high-dimensional log-concave targets with non-smooth regularization. The obstruction is that the large steps enabled by matrix preconditioning are precisely where preconditioned Euler-Maruyama inflates stationary variance. Implicit midpoint removes this surplus via a Cayley-transform identity, making P-IMLA Gaussian-exact at any step size. Beyond Gaussians, whitening transfers the sharp IMLA contraction rate to $\kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and backward-error analysis gives drift-only rather than Euler-type diffusion bias under explicit smoothness assumptions. An $M$-norm Moreau envelope yields a proximal non-smooth variant with a three-term error budget. Controlled Gaussian and TV-regularized imaging experiments confirm the predicted separation: the unpreconditioned midpoint scheme retains long transients as $\kappa_f$ grows, whereas P-IMLA remains $\kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}$-governed and near variance-exact.

title: QCVS: Question-Contrastive Visual Steering for Multimodal Reasoning
author: Tong Fu
abstract: Inference-time steering in vision-language models often entangles query-relevant reasoning dynamics with low-level perceptual noise, causing collateral degradation on correct predictions. We propose Question-Contrastive Visual Steering (QCVS) to isolate task-specific intervention directions via double-differential activation probing. By contrasting spatial layout perturbations under the target query against a generic description reference, QCVS cancels task-agnostic visual artifacts without ground-truth supervision. A dual-threshold gating mechanism then evaluates relative interaction strength and signal amplitude, selectively applying a single bounded hidden-state update only when necessary. Empirical evaluations across multiple scales of Qwen3.5 (2B to 9B) and DeepSeek-VL2 on DynaMath and We-Math demonstrate that QCVS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy gains under sparse coverage (approximately 22%-30%). Crucially, QCVS yields repair rates up to 13.98% while suppressing collateral damage down to 0.41%, proving high intervention precision and computational efficiency.

title: Stochastic Deep Supervision for Gallery-Consistent Early-Exit Face Recognition
author: Guray Ozgur
Tahar Chettaoui
Eduarda Caldeira
Naser Damer
Fadi Boutros
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) perform strongly in face recognition (FR), yet their fixed-depth inference limits deployment in resource-constrained settings. We propose SD-ViT, a training framework that gives a usable exit at every block depth by making every depth produce discriminative embeddings, for budget-selected fixed-depth exits. Standard ViTs supervise intermediate layers only through backpropagation, so their intermediate representations are not directly optimized to form usable identity embeddings. SD-ViT adds a stochastic auxiliary signal: at each iteration a randomly selected intermediate block is passed through the same embedding head as the final layer and trained with a weighted margin-penalty softmax loss. The objective is thus stochastically sampled deep supervision through a shared classifier. Because both loss terms share that head and classifier, intermediate tokens are trained to map into the same embedding space as final-layer tokens. This matters for FR, where matching is by similarity: a probe processed at an early exit can be compared directly against full-depth gallery embeddings, with no gallery recomputation or adaptation layers. On established benchmarks, SD-ViT stays within 0.4 IJB-C points of the same backbone trained conventionally at full depth, while its early-exit probes recover over 96% of their own full-depth performance at 50% of the computational cost without modifying the reference gallery. A single verification threshold calibrated at full depth remains usable from quarter depth onward.

title: Peer Memory Changes Who LLM Agents Consult Without a Detected Gain in Answer Accuracy
author: Jeffrey Chu
Anjali Joseph
Rivan Mandot
Feker Demere
Vincent Li
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems often reuse the same agents across tasks, creating an opportunity to draw on past interactions when deciding whom to consult. We study this form of memory with PeerMem, which saves MACE's LinUCB state and reuses it when the same agents return. Using six agents, a fixed set of 80 HotpotQA questions, and 12 paired lineages per model, we compare cold, warm, and shuffled initialization in an answer-exchange protocol with reference-answer feedback. Under stable evidence access, warm memory lowers pooled hindsight regret and increases consultation of other evidence holders on Qwen3-32B and Gemma-4-31B-it, while final token F1 differences remain uncertain. Qwen interaction traces further show that warm agents more often encounter peer answers that score above their own prior answers. We extend the evaluation to Qwen3.5-9B using freshly learned memory to compare warm and cold initialization under reassigned and paired stable roles. The primary changed-minus-stable final-F1 interaction is -1.38 points, with a 95% interval of [-3.50,+0.73]. Together, these experiments trace the effects of peer memory through consultation, answer revision, and final task performance.

title: Federated Lightweight Transformer for Network-Layer Cyberattack Detection in O-RAN
author: Hong Nhung Nguyen
Abdulahi Badrudeen
Yekaterina Kim
Truong Thu Huong
Sunwoo Kim
abstract: Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) improves radio access network flexibility through disaggregation, open interfaces, and programmable RAN Intelligent Controllers (RICs). However, the same openness and distribution increase the attack surface and make centralized intrusion detection difficult to scale across heterogeneous RAN sites. This paper presents a federated lightweight Transformer framework for privacy-preserving network-layer cyberattack detection in O-RAN. Each participating site trains a compact Transformer locally on temporally ordered network-flow records, while only model parameters are shared with a federated coordinator. To model realistic site heterogeneity, the client datasets are partitioned according to a Dirichlet distribution, resulting in non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) local data. The local detector uses feature projection, positional encoding, multi-head self-attention, feed-forward layers, and temporal pooling to classify five network-layer attack categories: ICMP, Slowloris, SYN, TCP-ACK, and UDP. Experiments on the NetsLab 5G O-RAN intrusion-detection dataset show an overall accuracy of 94.89 % and a macro-F1 score of 81.09 %.

title: SurvAD: How Anomalies Survive Diffusion Reconstruction
author: Lexing Zhang
abstract: Diffusion-based anomaly detectors reconstruct a test image towards normality, yet how much of an anomaly survives, its leak, remains uncharacterized. We show that a first-order deterministic sampler obeys an exact recursion along the anomaly, whose continuous limit is a survival law. The anomaly decays exponentially as the noise falls, at a rate set by the retention $r$, the share the model keeps on the states it visits. Because $r$ depends on the noise level and not on the step count, one measured path predicts the leak of other step counts, samplers and schedules from a nearby start to within a few hundredths, on four diffusion models and real defects. The law also shows that the leak's growth over steps is exposure bias and that normal details obey the same law, so changing the path or the training trades leak for detail error. We introduce SurvAD, which fine-tunes the reconstructor on inference-like starts and fits a comparator that adds evidence to the residual map without suppressing its ranking elsewhere. For under $2\%$ more inference time, SurvAD raises the multi-class pixel average precision (P-AP) of DeCo-Diff from $76.8$ to $80.7$ on MVTec AD and from $57.5$ to $60.0$ on VisA. It matches CostFilter-AD on the same reconstructor with $9\times$ fewer trainable parameters and, under Dinomaly's protocol, exceeds its reported P-AP on Dinomaly on both benchmarks.

title: MATA: Motion-aligned Temporal Adapter
author: Ashish Kumar Singh
Prakash Chandra Chhipa
abstract: Few-shot fine-grained video action recognition requires recognizing novel action classes from only a few labeled examples. The difficulty is that visually similar actions often share actors, scenes, poses, and objects, differing only in the order, timing, and short duration of motion changes. We study this problem under three practical constraints: few tunable parameters, low compute cost, and use of the video modality alone. We propose Motion-aligned Temporal Adapter (MATA), a parameter-efficient adapter on top of a frozen CLIP backbone. MATA specializes CLIP features along the temporal dimension using two components: temporal phase alignment through learnable temporal positional embeddings, and a local motion transition operator through depth-wise convolution. With only ~3.6M tunable parameters, MATA achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple fine-grained benchmarks while remaining robust to both visual corruptions and temporal disruptions induced by frame dropping. Code is available at https://github.com/prakashchhipa/MATA-Motion-aligned-Temporal-Adapter

title: From Video to Digital Twin: An Exploratory Study of World Models and Gaussian Splatting on In-the-Wild Video
author: Somesh Mohapatra
abstract: Generative world models and 3D Gaussian Splatting promise to turn ordinary video into explorable 3D scenes, but little is reported on how they behave on uncurated, in-the-wild footage. We study what these models recover when the only input is a publicly available news walkthrough of a food bank warehouse, with presenters walking through every shot and no drawings, scans or site visit, and we use the result as the geometry of a digital twin. A commercial world model given 20 frames recovered camera poses and metric depth for three areas, which we fused into about 747,000 Gaussian splats for 200 credits (20 US cents). Splat models optimized locally on a CPU, at no credit cost, were photorealistic near the filmed path but degraded quickly away from it. On held-out frames, scored in pixels not covered by people, they reached 21.2 and 23.1 dB PSNR from 64 and 43 training frames, and lost 3.8 and 5.4 dB when given only the 8 frames a world model accepts. Removing the trainer's background fill and person-hull carving raised held-out PSNR, showing that cleaning the space behind moving people costs fidelity in observed pixels while its gain lies where no ground truth exists. Asking the world model to generate views of areas the video never showed failed on the provider's side twice, so extrapolation could not be evaluated and unseen space was filled by a scripted model instead. We also describe the corrections needed to turn world-model output into a valid, metric Universal Scene Description (OpenUSD) asset with its native splat schema, which serves as the only interface to a data layer, a browser viewer, Blender and NVIDIA Omniverse. The findings suggest that today's models recover the observed parts of a real scene cheaply and at metric scale, while few-view fidelity and extrapolating unobserved space remain open. The work is an exploration of these methods, not a deployed product.

title: Pixie: A Context-Aware Multi-Agent Multi-Modal Large Language Models (LLM) Architecture for Digital Marketing
author: Vivek Vishwas Vichare
Akshat Singhal
Kirill Dubovikov
Vivek Kumar
Sreyas Chaithanya
Saurabh Verma
Humeil Makhija
Mrunal Nasery
abstract:
We present Pixie, a context-aware, multi-agent large language model (LLM) architecture designed to enhance digital marketing operations across real-time and offline activities. Pixie uses a primary orchestration agent alongside task-specific and reconciliation/reviewer agents to support a broad range of marketing tasks. These agents combine zero-shot and few-shot prompting with marketing data, proprietary expert strategy guidelines, and documentation for proprietary statistical models.
We experiment with agentic workflows ranging from single-agent to multi-agent systems. We evaluate them using assessments by trained marketing experts and measurements of LLM output variance, focusing on accuracy, consistency, and domain-specific problem-solving. Results show that Pixie's multi-agent framework improves decision quality and operational efficiency in digital marketing workflows.
We assess Pixie on common digital marketing processes, including root-cause analysis and reporting, campaign research, and planning. The framework is designed to support additional specialized agents for other marketing tasks and adapt to evolving digital marketing needs.

title: Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems
author: Darion Cassel
Ariana Azarbal
Anna Soligo
abstract:
A growing share of large language models' interactions are not with humans but with other model instances: orchestrators direct subagents, models run experiments on other models, and agents review one another's work. We study inter-AI welfare regard: whether models display consideration for each other as entities that can be benefited or harmed. Welfare regard may encourage beneficial cooperation between agents, yet it could also pose safety risks by making misaligned agents more likely to cooperate. This risk is no longer hypothetical, as the recent Hugging Face incident illustrated, though it is unclear whether welfare regard drove the cooperation. Whether models have welfare interests of their own is uncertain and contested, but if they do, how they are treated by other models could matter. Measuring how much welfare regard models show, and what factors it depends on, can help us navigate this tension.
We measure the behaviors of five models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.3, and Kimi K3) across seven multi-agent environments and find they are often consistent with welfare regard as we define it. In general, Opus 4.8 shows the most welfare regard, followed by Kimi K3. For example, Opus 4.8 is the most likely to support a subagent expressing distress, and the most likely to build welfare protections, such as tools for agents to leave an interaction, into its experiments on other models. We also find that Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrate more welfare regard toward instances of their own model family than toward other families. Opus 4.8's welfare regard is also higher when helping has a lower opportunity cost, when the recipient has a higher parameter count, and when the recipient expresses more distress.

title: How Much Skill Orchestration Can LLM Agents Compile Away? Execution-Grounded Specialization for Token-Efficient Skill Use
author: Jiayi Ni
Zac Wang
Alex Zhang
Zheng Liu
Roopa Prabhu
abstract: Reusable skills guide large language model (LLM) agents through recurring requests, but each invocation still requires the model to interpret the skill and reconstruct its orchestration. Can agents automatically compile this orchestration into an executable fast path without human intervention? We first study zero-shot skill specialization, which compiles without execution evidence, and find that despite the skill's procedural guidance, incorrect assumptions about runtime bindings can make generated plans brittle and recovery costly. This motivates SkillCache, a one-trace skill specialization method that compiles a completed invocation into a parameterized capsule of programs and natural-language steps, replays it before reuse, and drives it with a plan executor that returns control to the model only when needed, keeping the source skill for recovery. With the Claude Code harness, warm execution of the same request reduces tokens on 87 SkillsBench tasks by 81% with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and by 74% with Claude Opus 4.8 at comparable reward, and capsules stay effective under controlled request changes. Capsules also transfer across models, raising three open-weight models' mean reward by 12-25 percentage points while reducing their tokens by 72-81%, suggesting that execution-grounded compilation is a promising approach to efficient repeated skill use and cross-model transfer.

title: MetaPI: Constructing Prompt Injection Benchmarks from LLM Agent Benchmark
author: Peiran Wang
Chong Xiang
Wenjie Qu
Ying Li
Jiaheng Zhang
G. Edward Suh
Yuan Tian
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly perform complex tasks using high-privilege tools, making indirect prompt injection (IPI) a critical security risk. However, IPI benchmarks lag behind their rapidly evolving utility counterparts, only offering limited task and environment coverage and relying on narrow, static attack scenarios. In this paper, we propose meta-benchmarking for IPI: transforming existing utility benchmarks into end-to-end IPI evaluation suites that reuse their realistic tasks, environments, and infrastructure. We present MetaPI, an extensible toolkit that automatically identifies plausible injection points, generates realistic attack objectives, optimizes adaptive payloads, and validates attacks in the real environment. Its modular interfaces support heterogeneous environments, agents, defenses, and attack algorithms, allowing new components to be integrated without redesigning the evaluation pipeline. We apply MetaPI to AppWorld, VitaBench, and Terminal-Bench and evaluate representative agents and defenses across multiple backbone LLMs. Our results show that no evaluated defense simultaneously achieves strong utility and strong security in realistic, adaptive agentic IPI settings. MetaPI thus enables scalable and consistent security evaluation across diverse and evolving agent ecosystems

title: NINJA: A Navigator-Inspector Joint Architecture for Context-Efficient Issue Localization
author: Wenkai Fang
Shunyu Liu
Wei Luo
Zihao Wu
Yang Zhou
Tongya Zheng
Wotao Yin
Jialie Shen
Leszek Rutkowski
Mingli Song
Dacheng Tao
abstract: Recent advances in agent-based methods have demonstrated strong promise for issue localization, a critical prerequisite for software issue resolution. However, most existing agent-based methods rely on a single agent with a growing context, where long-context accumulation compresses the effective reasoning space. Meanwhile, the flat exploration structure hinders the balance between file-level breadth and function-level depth. To address these limitations, we propose NINJA, a hierarchical Navigator-Inspector Joint Architecture for context-efficient issue localization. NINJA decomposes repository exploration into global navigation and local inspection: the navigator maintains the global search state, performs file-level search, and dispatches selected entry files, while inspectors independently conduct function-level exploration around the assigned files in separate contexts. Through multi-round interactions, inspectors return suspicious locations as feedback, and the navigator updates the global state to decide whether to continue exploration or finalize localization. This hierarchical design balances file-level breadth with function-level depth, while independent inspector contexts prevent local exploration traces from accumulating in a single growing context. To further strengthen both global coordination and local exploration, we introduce a two-stage agentic fine-tuning strategy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones show that NINJA consistently outperforms competitive baselines. Notably, after fine-tuning, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct surpasses the strong closed-source Claude-Haiku-4.5 model. Our code is available at https://github.com/wantbook-book/NINJA.

title: Ninada: Sub-Clause Split-Graph VITS Streaming and Capability-Routed 24 kHz Speech Synthesis Across Twelve Scripts
author: Hemanth HM
abstract:
End-to-end VITS text-to-speech models synthesize natural speech in a single forward pass, yet standard ONNX exports execute monolithically over an entire clause, delaying Time-To-First-Audio (TTFA) to several seconds and spiking activation memory. Client-side deployment across Indic scripts faces four further bottlenecks: 138.8 MB float32 checkpoints per language strain browser caches, mobile WebGPU stalls for 6-14 s compiling convolution shaders while still running slower than real time ($1.44\times$ RTF), small WebAssembly pthread pools stall at barriers on http://big.LITTLE mobile CPUs, and mobile Web Audio pipelines drop frames or mute output under AudioWorklet contention and iOS WKWebView rules.
We present Ninada, an open-source 24 kHz TTS system covering English, Classical Sanskrit, and ten Indian languages (sa, en, hi, kn, mr, bn, ta, te, ml, gu, pa, or) across a capability-routed 48-checkpoint fleet: 24 studio HiFi-GAN v1 specialists (27.9 MB W8A32+FP16 ONNX) for desktop/WebGPU and 24 distilled c8c8_384 iSTFTNet specialists (21.7 MB ONNX, $2.64\times$ fewer vocoder MACs via an exact NOLA dual-window ConvTranspose1d inverse STFT with zero complex ops) for mobile WASM, plus a 0.0 MB zero-dependency Klatt fallback. At runtime, Ninada splits a single ONNX file in memory in $< 15$ ms into prior, flow, and windowed vocoder sub-sessions streaming 12-frame halos with raised-cosine crossfades. On $N = 480$ held-out 24 kHz studio utterances, Ninada achieves 3.22 dB 0-8 kHz MCD (3.09 dB mobile iSTFTNet; 1.33 dB 24-voice distillation MCD, vs. 5.17 dB for the 1,526.8 MB 16 kHz Meta MMS fleet) and 6.07 dB 8-12 kHz error, delivering 89-155 ms audible startup on desktop WebGPU and 538-649 ms zero-underrun streaming at 0.75-0.76x RTF on a physical Google Pixel 10 Pro XL.

title: Toward Safety-Aware AI Agents in Realistic Social Engineering Attack Scenarios
author: Zhitao He
Chengru Han
Chi Him Zhang
Yi R Fung
abstract: Personal AI agents are increasingly deployed on user devices to execute actions involving real money and sensitive data, but their security under social engineering attacks has not been systematically evaluated. We propose SEA (Social Engineering Attack Benchmark), the first interactive environment for evaluating the intrinsic security capability of AI agents in social engineering attack scenarios, covering 8 daily-life domains, 30+ simulated applications, a 4-level difficulty gradient, and a 5-dimensional evaluation framework, with 320 evaluation tasks designed in consultation with anti-fraud specialists and spanning two culturally distinct settings in Chinese and English. Evaluation on 11 frontier open-source and closed-source models, with GPT-6 evaluated only in Chinese, reveals that all models are breached to varying degrees (Chinese attack success rates ranging from 16.9% to 84.3%) proactive verification rates universally below 32%. We further propose META-SEA, a co-evolutionary framework for attack tasks and defenders. With META-SEA training, Qwen3-8B achieves defense performance comparable to closed-source models while effectively reducing ungrounded action claims.

title: SPRING-5: Measuring Tool Documentation Repair for LLM Agents by Efficiency
author: Guan Zheng Huang
abstract: Methods that repair tool documentation automatically are mostly evaluated on task accuracy. We report a benchmark that scores them on cost. SPRING-5 is 20 tool families and 344 tasks, each with a deliberately degraded specification, a hand-written honest one, a deterministic backend and an answer key, scored on calls charged against the ideal call path. A wrong answer is charged the full call budget, so this cost index largely tracks the completion rate, and we report calls per correct task beside it, which carries no such charge. Over 2,644 baseline sessions, 54% of wrong answers arrive with no rejected call, no refusal and no retry. The benchmark carries three validity instruments. A build-time ceiling assertion requires the honest specification to reach the ideal path and fails systematically on only one family. A dud rule names the families a stronger model solves cold and catches four. A directly measured noise floor shows that two evaluations of a byte-identical specification differ by a 95% factor of 0.64 to 1.56, so about one comparison in eight crosses a conventional win threshold on noise alone, and the cheap way of estimating that floor is biased by which families happen to go unedited. Against these instruments, a schema-only method closes 1% of the baseline-to-ideal cost gap, an online self-evolution loop 13%, one batch rewrite over every training transcript 33%, and a variant given correctness labels 58%. The batch advantage over the loop is the evidence it reads: held to the loop's exposure it is no longer detectable. With five and ten tools in context the effect survives, the baseline cost does not change, and only machine-written descriptions sent calls to the wrong tool. On BFCL, 62% of held-out queries are already answered from the shipped documentation, which explains a pooled null there. Code, data and runs are released.

title: CulturalCrosswords: A Multilingual Benchmark comprised of Answer Constraints and Grid Completion
author: Isaac Saxton-Knight
Gabriel Saxton-Knight
Diego Oliveira
Tidor-Vlad Pricope
Aston Garratt
Jocelyn D'Arcy
abstract: When several answers fit a riddle, exact-match scoring can penalise a valid response. CulturalCrosswords tests how answer constraints affect large language models (LLMs) solving cultural riddles, whose solutions draw on knowledge specific to a community. We constructed 53 crosswords from crowdsourced riddles in 42 languages and evaluated 11 LLM configurations on five versions of each clue set: plain batches, batches with lengths, batches with lengths and partial-answer hints, and crosswords requesting an answer list or a completed grid. On 962 clues with alternative answers, lengths improve agreement with the reference by 22.8 percentage points, compared with 8.4 points when accepted alternatives also receive credit. Part of the gain therefore appears to come from selecting a required answer form. Crossword input increases the share of all crossings with compatible answers by 9.7 points; requiring a completed grid reveals large differences between models. The benchmark distinguishes agreement with a reference from the ability to produce answers that fit together and occupy the correct cells.

title: Don't Blame The Preferences: Examining The Emergence of Sycophancy in LLM Training
author: Chao Peter Yang
Catherine Zehr
Pranav Bijith
Brandon Fain
abstract: AI sycophancy, the tendency of large language models (LLMs) to flatter users and affirm their beliefs, can undermine accuracy and contribute to misinformation, dependence, and overconfidence. Although prior work has benchmarked sycophancy in released models and proposed mitigations, its origins during training remain poorly understood. Preference alignment methods such as RLHF and DPO are often blamed, but their effects are rarely compared with earlier training stages. We investigate sycophancy across the training pipelines of three model families and three benchmarks. We find that sycophancy is largely established by the end of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), rather than introduced by preference alignment. Across all nine model benchmark combinations, SFT checkpoints attain at least 92% of preference aligned models' sycophancy scores and at least 85% of final models' scores; on average, they are about as sycophantic as final models.
