We further identify a planning-horizon asymmetry between long-horizon top-level composition and short two-step subordinate planning. To address these challenges, we propose WARP-JEPA, a hierarchical amortized planning framework that replaces online gradient optimization with learned multi-candidate trajectory proposers while keeping the world models frozen. WARP-JEPA combines a lightweight world-model-in-the-loop causal Transformer at the top level with parallel residual MLPs at subordinate levels. The proposers are trained using model-based rollout costs and best-of-K behavior cloning, enabling efficient candidate selection without test-time gradient optimization. Across 30 frozen H-JEPA models on four benchmarks, WARP-JEPA achieves 9.6-18.8x faster episode inference on long-horizon tasks (2.9-3.0x on Cube) and improves task success by up to 33.3 percentage points. These results demonstrate that amortized planning can substantially improve both inference efficiency and control performance without retraining the world models. Code is available at https://github.com/hideinsewer/WARP-JEPA.

title: CompAIssionate Other: Identity Assumptions in LLM Responses to Distress
author: Drishti Goel
Ethan M. Nguyen
Violeta J. Rodriguez
Koustuv Saha
abstract: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.

title: Selective Cooperative Perception via Blind Spot Reasoning and Agentic Dialogue with Vision-Language Models
author: Chengyuan Ma
Shixiao Liang
Hangyu Li
Zheng Li
Hang Zhou
Keke Long
Bofeng Cao
Zhaohui Liang
Xiaopeng Li
abstract: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.

title: Learning When to Think: Adaptive Internal Computation for Reinforcement Learning
author: Rohit Kumar Salla
Simon Stepputtis
abstract: Iterative neural policies usually spend the same computation on every decision, although the benefit of additional processing varies across states. We introduce Adaptive Internal Computation (AIC), an iterative policy that learns when to stop refining its latent representation and act. In AIC, we train action selection and stopping jointly, an expected-depth penalty values computation and intermediate value predictions provide auxiliary supervision. We show that when only some states benefit from further refinement, an ideal state-dependent allocator outperforms every state-independent stopping schedule at the same expected depth. With at most eight refinement steps per decision, AIC executes 3.3 steps on average across twelve benchmark tasks and lowers per-decision latency by 31--44% relative to a fixed eight-step policy on four control and robotics tasks. Its mean reward exceeds the best fixed-depth policy on seven tasks and trails it on four. Ablating adaptive stopping and value supervision separately shows that stopping accounts for most of the reward gain on PickCube and AntMaze, where it also executes more refinement steps and that supervision accounts for most of it on RareEvent.

title: AutoC2V: Synthesis-Guided LLM Training for QoR-Optimized C++-to-Verilog Generation
author: Guanqi Lyu
Fei Zhao
Zhaojun Lu
Jiaji He
Yongqiang Lyu
abstract: High-level synthesis (HLS) can translate C/C++ kernels into register-transfer level (RTL) designs, yet generating high-quality hardware still relies heavily on manual pragma tuning and repeated synthesis evaluation. We propose AutoC2V, a C++-to-Verilog generation framework driven by real synthesis feedback that enables large language models (LLMs) to directly generate RTL with improved quality of results (QoR) from synthesizable C++ kernels. We construct training data from real synthesis results, including synthesizable C++ source code, the corresponding Verilog RTL, QoR metrics, and optimization objectives. Using this dataset, we align the model toward synthesis-aware RTL generation through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To reduce the high cost of repeatedly invoking real synthesis during GRPO, we design the QoR Prediction Reward Model (QoR RM), which predicts latency and resource metrics by encoding RTL into long-context semantic representations, thereby providing low-cost and continuous QoR reward signals for policy optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that AutoC2V not only substantially improves RTL functional pass rates, but also achieves superior latency and resource optimization compared to the unfine-tuned base model, representative HLS optimization approaches (HLSPilot, LLM-DSE, and AutoDSE), and advanced general-purpose commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek v4 Pro, and GLM-5.2). These results indicate that combining real synthesis data with efficient QoR reward modeling can further improve the ability of LLMs to generate high-quality RTL.

title: MoE-DAgger: Transition-Aware Router-Entropy Gating for Selective Human Correction in Phase-Structured Manipulation
author: Sungjun Heo
Sungjun Yang
Heedon Jeong
Junhyoung Ha
Jeong hwan Jeon
abstract: Selective data acquisition in Dataset Aggregation (DAgger) on robots requires deciding which learner rollouts to correct and when to intervene. In manipulation with ordered phases, router entropy from a phase-supervised soft mixture-of-experts (MoE) is insufficient: the same value can reflect either a normal adjacent-phase handoff or support for nonadjacent or earlier phases. We propose MoE-DAgger, which uses causal router history to distinguish these cases without providing the policy with a phase label, progress variable, or hard phase command during execution. The acquisition rule allows an adjacent transition to settle, but requests correction when high entropy persists outside such a transition, the transition times out, or routing persistently favors an earlier phase. Under matched active human-control budgets, MoE-DAgger achieves 84.0% task success on Green and 78.0% on Red, exceeding phase-unaware filtered entropy by 22 percentage points on Green and 26 points on Red, with no observed collisions in 50 rollouts per task. On 50 shared intervention-free traces per task, 83.3% and 80.0% of its first proposals fall on failed rollouts within predefined failure windows when 15 and 25 traces are selected, compared with 70.0% and 72.0% for temporal action-chunk disagreement and 63.3% and 60.0% for ensemble disagreement. Shadow replay and an active no-veto ablation indicate that suppressing queries at normal adjacent handoffs is a key contributor to the improved allocation.

title: The Devil Wears Markdown: Detecting Malicious Intent Hidden in AI Agent Skill Instructions through Hybrid Static, Dynamic, and Agentic Analysis
author: Thanh M. Truong-Le
Amber Bennoui
Hoang-Ly Nguyen
Gia-Thang Ho
Thai-Minh Truong
Duc-Ly Vu
abstract:
Agentic AI ecosystems increasingly rely on reusable agent skills that combine executable code, natural-language instructions, configuration artifacts, and external tool integrations. These hybrid artifacts create software supply-chain risks because malicious intent may be distributed across instructions, code, metadata, and runtime behavior, making isolated alerts difficult to interpret.
We evaluate three open-source scanners on a held-out test set of 140 skills comprising 80 malicious and 60 benign samples, including Cisco Skill Scanner with and without its optional LLM analyzer. The default Cisco configuration achieves a recall of 0.91 with 33 false positives among the 60 benign skills, while the LLM-enabled configuration using Qwen3:8B achieves a recall of 0.85 with 40 false positives.
We then present a framework that combines static findings, safety-constrained sandbox evidence, and LLM-based reasoning to assess malicious intent. The framework tracks the origins of findings and relates evidence across analysis layers. In a within-system evidence-source ablation using the same reasoning backend, adding dynamic evidence to skill-content reasoning increases F1 from 0.70 to 0.85. Combining static and dynamic evidence further increases F1 to 0.89, with five false positives among 60 benign skills. Dynamic evidence provides the largest observed improvement.
The Full Pipeline detects 68 of 80 malicious skills, achieving 0.88 accuracy, 0.93 precision, and 0.85 recall. It matches the observed recall of Cisco Skill Scanner with LLM while reducing false positives from 40 to five. This system-level comparison does not isolate model or architecture effects.

title: Multimodal Models Can See, But Can They Think? A Study of Turkish Visual Reasoning
author: Berke Bunyamin Sule
Yavuz Selim Aygan
Ahmed Zeer
Elif Ince
Ali Mert Temizsoy
Ozgur Agar
Himmet Toprak Kesgin
Muzaffer Kaan Yuce
Mehmet Fatih Amasyali
abstract: Vision-Language Models have had massive leaps in recent years. Yet, when tested on high-level cognitive tasks like pattern completion, abstract logic, and relational reasoning, they still fall short. This limitation stems from the models' lack of ability to find out underlying rules and maintain constant intermediate steps, rather than merely deciding on the correct option. To research these shortcomings, this study analyzes visual reasoning performance throughout a multilingual evaluation framework encompassing the BÄ°LSEM, MM-IQ, Visual Puzzles, and PuzzleVQA datasets. We evaluate various data mixing strategies and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) methods. We observed that a correct answer does not always mean the reasoning chain is valid. Because of this, we adopt an LLM-as-a-Judge approach to assess the quality of reasoning beyond final answer accuracy. Our experimental results reveal that baseline models often exhibit more stable reasoning compared to fine-tuned counterparts. Most importantly, we observe that SFT can lead to model collapse, manifesting as infinite text loops or empty outputs. The study concludes that current VLMs still struggle with abstract visual reasoning.

title: Firepool: Brokering Warm GPU Capacity for Agentic and RL Workloads at LinkedIn
author: Ankit Goyal
Santosh Jha
Zhuo Zhi
Youmin Han
Cong Gu
Chen Xie
Animesh Singh
abstract: AI agents and reinforcement-learning (RL) trainers run thousands of short, isolated GPU jobs: tool calls, verifiers, and rollouts. A job often finishes in seconds, but starting a GPU pod for it takes 20-35 s even when the container image is already on the node, and minutes when it is not. A warm pod removes the wait only if it can serve the next job, and keeping pods warm must neither waste GPUs nor leak state between callers. Firepool, the sandbox and execution broker behind agentic and RL workloads at LinkedIn, meets both requirements. It makes pods interchangeable by building them from a shared base image per hardware profile and binding each job's code, extra dependencies, and cluster topology when the job starts. It keeps them warm cheaply and safely by reusing a pod only for the caller that used it last, staging zero-VRAM standby pods in fractional GPU shares alongside active pods, and capping the GPUs that warm pools may hold via queue-driven budgets. Over a sampled peak period in production, Firepool serves 94.7% of 3,206 pod requests from warm or standby capacity. In paired benchmarks with fixed-duration jobs on production H200 nodes, agent and RL loops finish 13x and 10.8x faster than with a fresh pod per job; against a fresh reuse tag per job, warm reuse cuts p90 start latency from 59.1 s to 3.5 s. When a job cannot reuse the previous pod, standby promotion shortens the handover wait from 51 s to 0.94 s. In local and simulated runs, a keep-alive matched to the loop's pauses keeps the latency benefit while holding about half the capacity of an always-on pool.

title: Simple Test-Time Refinement for Plot-to-Code Generation via Visual-Code Diagnostics
author: Peiming Guo
Jinpeng Huang
Yangbin Sun
Gaoxiong Cao
Ensheng Shi
Yuchi Ma
Yu Zhang
Meishan Zhang
Baotian Hu
Min Zhang
abstract: Plot-to-code generation has been greatly advanced by recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing studies mainly focus on one-pass generation or iterative sampling guided by verifier-based filtering, which does not align with the typical human programming workflow of generate first, then iteratively error-location and fix. This naturally motivates a test-time refinement paradigm for plot-to-code generation. In this work, we present the first study on plot-to-code generation via iterative test-time refinement. We propose a Visual-Code Diagnostics framework that enables refinement through visual feedback from source code. Specifically, we first categorize generation errors into four coarse-grained types, and then train lightweight discriminators to recognize and localize these errors based on the rendered visual outputs and corresponding code. Unlike traditional compiler- or debugger-based verification, our approach performs iterative refinement guided by one diagnostics system, enabling more effective semantic and visual correction during test time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently improves generation quality across diverse generators and significantly outperforms strong test-time scaling baselines.

title: A Gamified Framework for Conflict-Driven Design: Discovering Strategies for Collaborative Resilience with Multi-Agent Learning
author: Jin Gao
abstract: Conflicting stakeholder objectives make it difficult to coordinate investments in urban resilience. We model conflict-driven urban design as a non-zero-sum digital board game in which stakeholder agents allocate scarce resources and balance individual payoffs against shared urban development and resilience objectives. We use multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to train policies and examine their behavior across three settings. On a 4 x 4 board, learned policies reach about 84% of the total return found by a simulated annealing benchmark. On an 8 x 8 board with spatial and resource constraints, trained agents favor projects that improve resilience in self-play. In a 12 x 12 simulation initialized from historical maps of Tatsumi, Tokyo, trained agents achieve a mean total score of 452.1, compared with 357.3 for a random-policy baseline across 10,000 simulation runs. Gains in adaptability, sustainability, flood resistance, and greenery come with reductions in vitality and density. A human-in-the-loop interface supports replay and lets participants take over stakeholder decisions, providing a testbed for exploring these trade-offs in participatory urban planning.

title: Agents of Chaos: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on Malicious Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
author: Thanh M. Truong-Le
Amber Bennoui
Hoang-Ly Nguyen
Gia-Thang Ho
Thai-Minh Truong
Duc-Ly Vu
abstract:
Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, retrieval, browser or computer-use interfaces, code execution, external services, and multi-agent coordination. Although these capabilities enable agents to act beyond text generation and perform tasks, they also create attack paths through which adversaries can exploit untrusted content, deceptive metadata, poisoned state, compromised skills, mutable dependencies, or malicious code. Such attacks can manipulate planning and tool use, corrupt memory, abuse code-execution environments, and trigger harmful downstream effects.
In this paper, we present a systematic review of malicious attacks targeting agentic AI systems. We screened 186 candidate sources and retained 98. Following independent coding and resolver adjudication, we identified 284 atomic attacks, 452 atomic safeguards, and 660 explicit attack--safeguard relationships. We organize attacks into eight causal-mechanism classes while retaining insertion points, activation conditions, abused capabilities, objectives, impacts, persistence, and evidence as orthogonal dimensions.
Our analysis shows that tool, MCP, and action-layer attacks account for the largest share of atomic attacks, while the prompt-injection and action-hijacking class has the broadest paper coverage. We identify distinct class-specific activation patterns and separation between insertion and later activation. Safeguard coverage remains uneven: only 278 of 660 relationships are directly assessed, and strong coverage is uncommon. These findings support lifecycle-aware threat modeling, agent evaluation, tool governance, and defense-in-depth security for agentic AI systems.

title: What Broke & Why: Practical Lessons from Reinforcement Learning Post-Training
author: Luv Verma
abstract:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an important way to improve how language models reason, solve problems, and use tools. But getting it to work in practice is not always straightforward. Training can fail because a model receives no useful reward, learns to exploit the reward system, stops exploring, or appears to improve when the evaluation itself is misleading.
In this book, we give a practical introduction to reinforcement learning post-training for language models, focusing on what works, what fails, and why. We begin with the foundations of post-training, explain GRPO and the training loop step by step, and then follow five training programs covering math reasoning, search agents, training stability, mixture-of-experts models, and software engineering tasks. Each program shows the problems encountered, the changes made, and the lessons learned.
The book also examines what reinforcement learning actually changes inside a model. The remaining chapters provide a practical reference for reward design, evaluation, training tool-using agents, debugging common failures, reproducibility, rollout engines, and hardware. Written for researchers and practitioners working with open models, the book aims to help readers understand how to train models, recognize when something goes wrong, and decide what to try next.

title: Fine-resolution land-use segmentation and synthetic image-label augmentation in the Kathmandu Valley
author: Pranil Parajuli
Sugam Dahal
Kiran Chandra Dahal
abstract: Parcel-scale land-use data is missing for most rapidly urbanizing Global South cities, as current segmentation architectures rely on multispectral imagery and planned layouts. We introduce a hand-annotated six-class land-use corpus covering 202 km$^2$ of Kathmandu Valley across 408 fine-resolution RGB scenes. The dataset is uniquely challenging: RGB spectral similarity is high, class imbalance approaches 100:1, and key structural features like rivers measure just two to three pixels wide at a standard hierarchical decoder's prediction stride. Evaluating five architectures reveals that standard random data splitting conceals massive spatial leakage. Switching to a strict sequence-block split drops performance by up to 0.095 mIoU. This penalty exceeds the performance gap between the architectures themselves. We modified the SegFormer baseline by integrating a half-resolution residual detail path, boundary-reliability reweighting, a topology-aware loss, and a presence-balanced sampler. Adding only 1.9% more parameters, the enhanced architecture improves mean IoU across every test fold, with gains concentrated in rare, thin-structure classes. However, both models achieve identical results on the external LoveDA benchmark. Finally, augmenting with diffusion-generated pairs at matched compute degraded accuracy across all architectures, especially harming rare classes it aimed to improve. This demonstrates that blindly incorporating synthetic data can severely damage performance, highlighting a critical need to rigorously evaluate and filter generated samples before training.

title: MultiTurnRoute: A Platform for Building and Evaluating Multi-Turn LLM Routers
author: Jiaqi Xue
Mengxin Zheng
Heng Huang
Qian Lou
abstract: In a multi-turn conversation, the choice of language model at one turn can affect which model should answer the next. The selected model's reply shapes the context for the next query, and its cached prompt prefix can reduce the cost of using that model again. We introduce MultiTurnRoute, a platform for building and evaluating multi-turn LLM routers. A shared interface gives built-in and user-defined routers the current query, dialogue history, and an estimate of each model's reusable prefix length. Our routing algorithm, Chain-of-Route (CoR), uses a learned gate over recent and recurrent dialogue history to predict response quality and estimates cost from each model's reusable prefix. MultiTurnRoute Arena ranks routers on recorded conversations and compares session quality and cost in interactive runs where a simulated user responds to each reply. On a benchmark drawn from WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M with per-turn quality annotations for five LLMs, CoR reduces the normalized cost required to match the strongest model's quality by up to 20.3% relative to the strongest routing baseline, while matching or improving peak response quality.

title: Polynomial Denoisers on the Image Manifold: Volterra Networks for Self-Contained Pixel Diffusion
author: Siddharth Roheda
Rohit Chowdhury
Amit Satish Unde
Aniruddha Bala
abstract: Natural images are often conjectured to lie on a low-dimensional manifold within the high-dimensional pixel space. Recent work leverages this to build self-contained pixel-space diffusion models without specialized machinery or pretrained components. A plain Transformer on raw image patches suffices, provided it predicts the clean image rather than the noise and compresses each patch through an aggressive bottleneck. The mixing operator, however, has remained softmax attention, inherited from sequence modeling rather than derived from denoising. For Gaussian noise, the optimal denoiser admits a canonical expansion in polynomial functionals of the observation, the Wiener--Volterra series. We prove that softmax attention, and any normalized mixing rule (including linear attention), cannot realize any polynomial map beyond an affine one. In contrast, Volterra layers realize this class directly and, on a data manifold, achieve approximation rates governed by the manifold dimension rather than the ambient pixel dimension. We therefore propose the architecture these results prescribe; raw image patches passed through a bottleneck embedding, followed by cascaded low-rank Volterra layers, which carry no activation function because each layer is nonlinear in its own right. To our knowledge this is the first pixel-space diffusion architecture whose mixing operators are Volterra layers throughout, with no attention, no convolution, no pretrained components, and no activation function on the residual path. On ImageNet $256 \times 256$ and $512 \times 512$, the resulting model is competitive with self-contained pixel-space diffusion at matched parameter and FLOP budgets.

title: Stochastic Port-Hamiltonian Gaussian Processes for Learning from Noisy Dynamics on Lie Groups
author: Thribhuvan Rapolu
Luke McLennan
Chandrajit Bajaj
abstract: Learning predictive models for dynamics is difficult because observations are often sparse and noisy, while the underlying dynamics evolve on nonlinear configuration manifolds and are affected by environmental dissipation and stochastic disturbances. Standard neural dynamics models can fit short-term trajectories but often violate physical structure, accumulate error over long horizons, or rely on parameterizations that introduce singularities such as gimbal lock. We introduce LieSPHGP, a stochastic Gaussian-process framework for learning rigid body dynamics with port-Hamiltonian structure and stability-aware robustness. LieSPHGP represents motion on Lie groups and Lie algebras, enabling coordinate-consistent optimization without singular parameterizations. Learned mass, potential energy, dissipation, and control components retain physical roles and a separate diffusion term represents stochastic forcing. Each component is modeled by MatÃ©rn kernel Gaussian processes which capture uncertainty induced by noisy observations. To improve physical validity, Lie group exponential map updates preserve rotational constraints, while positive-definite damping ensures nonnegative deterministic energy dissipation. The implicit-explicit integrator additionally provides unconditional stability for the frozen linear damping subsystem. The resulting model learns predictive dynamics that are robust to noise, respect rigid body geometry, and capture both intrinsic motion and environmental dissipation. Experiments on various noisy rigid body benchmarks show improved prediction accuracy, stronger long-horizon stability, and better satisfaction of manifold constraints compared with neural dynamics baselines. Code, data and interactive results are available on the project website: https://thribhuvanrapolu.github.io/liesphgp/

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
author: Jack Lu
Zhenbang Yang
Mike Lasby
Tejas Pote
Yani Ioannou
Mengye Ren
abstract: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.

title: DreamVLA: From Generated Human Motions to Humanoid Vision-Language-Action Policies
author: Kevin Park
Izat Rasyad
Dvij Kalaria
Shankar Sastry
abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically depends on substantial robot demonstration data, making human teleoperation a costly and cumbersome bottleneck, particularly for whole-body humanoid interaction. Reinforcement learning in simulation offers an alternative for scaling this data, but designing task-specific rewards remains challenging. To address this, we propose DreamVLA, which uses generated motion trajectories to guide reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, converting them into reliable task execution trajectories. These trajectories train VLA models in simulation without new task-specific teleoperation data. Our central contribution is a reference-conditioned DAgger distillation procedure: after a failed learner rollout, we restart the RL expert from a sampled learner state with the same reference suffix and aggregate successful corrective trajectories, addressing the distribution shift left by offline imitation. We evaluate picking from a platform, opening a drawer, pressing a button, and walking and picking from a platform, with ablations of DAgger iterations, residual RL, and generated dataset scale. Project website: http://ember-center-berkeley.github.io/DreamVLA.

title: BRAT: Bounded Residual-Aligned Training for Stable Multi-Pass LLM Post-Training
author: Xunlan Zhou
Yuzhe Zhao
Xuhong Huang
Feng Chen
Xuanlin Chen
Lang Feng
Bo An
abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language model post-training often reuses each batch of sampled rollouts for several gradient passes to amortize the cost of generation. Under such multi-pass reuse, existing objectives fail in different ways: unclipped updates collapse as the policy drifts away from the sampling policy, adding a negative baseline avoids collapse but reinforces every sampled response, and PPO-style ratio clipping cuts off gradients abruptly. We first ask why reuse is fragile. Measuring how well an update estimated from a small rollout group aligns with the KL-regularized target on held-out rollouts of the same prompts, we find that this alignment drops by nearly an order of magnitude from in-sample to held-out rollouts across three base models, suggesting that repeated passes largely overfit the sampled group. Motivated by this finding, we propose Bounded Residual-Aligned Training (BRAT), motivated by a proximal update toward a bounded reweighting of the sampling policy. BRAT assigns each token a gradient weight that decreases linearly with its probability ratio and vanishes at a trust-region boundary, and normalizes group-centered rewards by their maximum magnitude, keeping advantages zero-mean and bounded without extra hyperparameters. With four reuse passes, BRAT avoids training collapse, limits policy drift, and achieves higher average accuracy with lower seed variance on most benchmarks.

title: Keeping LLM Agents on Procedure: Executable Finite-State Control for Long-Horizon Instruction Fidelity
author: Yutao Sun
Haokun Li
Mingshuai Chen
Guanyan Li
Zhongyi Wang
Shengchao Qin
Jianwei Yin
abstract: Much of the automation handed to language-model agents is procedural: each step needs little intelligence, but a long unattended run must follow a skill or SOP stated once at the start. We show that agents drift from such procedures over long runs, and that restating the instructions or resuming a stopped agent only moves the drift to another shortcut. We study an executable finite-state machine (FSM) that keeps the workflow state outside the model's context and enforces it at three points: tool calls, state transitions and the end of the agent's turn. In a pre-registered experiment on 200-account SOP-Bench batches, Claude Haiku 4.5 with the FSM decided on average 139 accounts correctly and by the procedure, against 48 for the strongest baseline (95% CI of the difference [46, 130]), and kept this rate to the end; across three models, the gain tracked how much the plain agent drifted. Because the runtime, not the model, supplies this long-horizon reliability, the FSM can let small models carry procedural work: Haiku 4.5 with it averaged more such decisions than plain Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 38% of the cost. Analyses on SWE-bench Verified, $\tau^2$-bench, and staged and cross-context workflows further suggest that reliable long-horizon automation can come from stronger execution control, not only stronger models.

title: Approximate Recall, Approximate Forecasts: Recall as a Diagnostic for LLM Forecasting Errors
author: Prashanth Bhaskara
Shubhaankar Gupta
Seojoon Yeon
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit approximate recall: they retain coarse associations about past events while losing fidelity on specific details. Past research on LLMs has quantified different models' forecasting ability in real-world events using prediction markets, but has not studied how losing said fidelity impacts their forecasting abilities. For example: while an LLM correctly recalls that the answer to: ''Did Anna Sawai win the Best Drama Actress in the 76th Emmy Awards?'' is ''Yes,'' it incorrectly states the event date as September 22 rather than September 15. In this paper, we introduce a novel metric called the Recall Fidelity Score to study how imprecision in internalized knowledge propagates to forecasting capability on future events. On resolved historical markets, we find that higher local recall fidelity around semantically similar past events predicts lower forecasting error on resolved markets, and the same signal predicts smaller distance from open markets prices.

title: Zero-Shot VLA Adaptation with Retrieved Guidance
author: Subin Kim
Anh-Quan Pham
Dinesh Jayaraman
abstract: Pre-training large parametric "Vision-Language-Action" (VLA) models on large demonstration datasets has recently yielded promising results for general-purpose manipulation. However, these models still struggle under even small domain shifts relative to the training data, such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity, or robot morphology. Motivated by the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in language models, we pursue retrieval to boost VLA performance. Specifically, we seek to leverage retrieval from domain-mismatched, "in-the-wild" demonstration datasets like DROID to guide a VLA's behavior in a new target domain. To achieve this, we introduce RAGu, which overcomes robotics-specific challenges for RAG: (1) It incorporates simple geometric calibration to transform source demonstrations into the target setup and reduce cross-domain differences. (2) It uses a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy that selects, from a large pool of pre-warped candidates, the trajectory most compatible with the base VLA. (3) It guides the VLA's flow-matching inference procedure rather than seeking to retrain the base model or expand its limited context window. We evaluate RAGu across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real transfer, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation. We find it improves real-world VLA success rates from 20% to 80% and outperforms the closest-related baselines in sim. Project website: http://raguvla.github.io

title: Beyond Real or Fake: A Dual-Channel Authenticity and Reasoning Protocol for Photographic Assessment
author: Xiaoxiao Li
Ruinan Jin
Lili Meng
Miaosen Wang
Athula Balachandran
Pei Cao
abstract: Forensic verification has converged on a binary "real vs. fake" label that confates fully synthetic, tampered, and AI-retouched images despite their very different consequences. We argue that GenAI manipulations decompose along two complementary channels: a camera channel of sensor fingerprints (destroyed by neural processing), and a semantic channel of scene-level coherence (disrupted by content edits). Each manipulation type leaves a distinctive two-channel signature. We instantiate this taxonomy in 2CAP (2-Channel Authenticity Protocol), pairing a contrastively-trained camera encoder with a frozen semantic encoder to serve two applications on a shared backbone: (i) four-class authenticity classification via cross-attention fusion with learnable reliability weights; and (ii) evidence generation, where an authentic image serves as a reference for a query and the two encoders produce per-channel alignment scores together with a patch-level saliency map. These signals are supplied as privileged context to a frozen Vision-Language Model (VLM) through an Observe-Generate-Refine loop, yielding explanations with localization without forensic fine-tuning. On a multi-source benchmark, 2CAP attains the best classification performance, including strong retouching detection where existing methods fail, and improves explanation quality.

title: Pole or Vector? Encoders Capture Bangla Compound Verbs, but LLMs Read Them Literally
author: Md. Asaduzzaman Shuvo
Md Mehrab Karim Antor
Md. Adnanul Islam
Shahanur Rahman Bappy
Sajid Ahamed
Mahfuz Hasan Reza
Md Delwar Shahadat Deepu
abstract: In Bangla, a main verb is often followed by one of a small set of vector verbs. These verbs lose their own meaning and add a shade of meaning instead, such as completion. For example, likhe phello means that someone finished writing, not that they wrote and threw something. The same two verbs can also describe two separate events, so only the context shows which meaning is meant. This makes compound verbs a hard test of how language models handle multiword expressions. We present BanglaCV-Probe, a benchmark of 17 vector verbs with 1,044 minimal pairs, 204 entailment items and 197 pairs of correct and incorrect combinations, all checked by native speakers. We test 26 models (encoders, LLMs and translation systems) on four skills: telling the two meanings apart internally, understanding what a vector adds, preferring correct combinations and keeping the vector's meaning in translation. Probes on five encoders tell the two meanings apart and still reach up to 93% accuracy when trained on pairs without surface cues. Prompted models rarely use this knowledge. Entailment accuracy stays between 59% and 81%. Several LLMs answer Yes or No to almost every item, and nine of ten models miss that someone who ate up the rice left none. Most instruction-tuned LLMs translate vectors literally in 15-20% of vector sentences and in up to 55% for mora (die). On correct combinations, a small Bangla-only model (88%) matches BLOOM-7B1 (87%) and both beat Qwen2.5-7B (74%). Data and code: https://github.com/ashuvo25/Pole_OR_Vector

title: DeepFinance: Can AI Diligence a $100MM Deal?
author: Drew Hahn
Tyler Shibata
Jackson Grove
Rahul Sonwalkar
abstract: Existing evaluations of AI models on high-finance work focus on retrieving answers from financial documents and producing numerically correct outputs. Real private equity (PE) and investment banking (IB) work also depends on choosing between conflicting sources, making sound assumptions, and keeping every step auditable. We introduce DeepFinance, an ultra long-horizon benchmark of 21 end-to-end PE and IB tasks that take a human professional an average of 27.1 hours. Each task pairs a request with a data room averaging 19 files and is graded against an average of 84 expert-written rubric criteria covering output, workflow, and judgment. We evaluate 22 model configurations, each in its native agent harness. The best configuration, GPT-6 Astra with max reasoning, satisfies 57.6% of rubric criteria, and the top four configurations are not statistically distinguishable. Frontier models often calculate correctly from the wrong inputs and find decision-relevant evidence without acting on it.

title: Beating the Pool, Not the Game: A White-Box Equilibrium Agent for Language-Based Economic Games
author: Sudhanshu Srivastava
Faisal Aqlan
abstract: We describe sudsho, a rule-based agent for the GLEE Competition that plays bargaining, negotiation, and persuasion with zero inference-time LLM calls. Games are scored as payoff percentiles against an empirical pool of prior play on the same configuration, so pool percentiles set our demand targets while clamped equilibrium shares bound demands and acceptance. Every move is a deterministic function of the visible state (persuasion mixing aside), so alignment is verified by replaying the post-freeze move log through the policy. Across 117,280 games the agent reached an overall rating of 2056 at $0 inference cost, and the account, ranked by its best agent (a same-policy replica), placed 26th of 71 ranked accounts. A replay against three frozen snapshots of the opponent pool credits the pool-aware clamp with 274 to 330 points of mean per-game bargaining rating, an effect that holds where logged opponent decisions fix the replay.

title: Can small transformers learn the language of Coxeter groups?
author: J. Elisenda Grigsby
Yiyao Huang
Arushi Katyal
Ryan Lin
Pranav Ramakrishnan
Weiya Wang
abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability is well-suited to collaborative projects between mathematicians and AI researchers. This work describes one such project. We trained a small transformer to learn the language of the Coxeter group affine A2, best known as the symmetries of the tiling of the Euclidean plane by equilateral triangles. We then formulated and proved a word-theoretic conjecture about affine A2 after observing the attention patterns of the trained model.

title: BRACE: Belief-guided Residual Adaptive Control for Safe Navigation under Unknown Disturbances
author: Jaeyoun Choi
Niklas Schmid
Oswin So
Augustinos Saravanos
Chuchu Fan
abstract: Disturbances encountered during autonomous navigation generally vary across space, often discontinuously, as obstacles redirect wind and changing terrain alters traction. Tracking controllers typically assume sufficient control authority to mitigate disturbances and maintain safety; the regime where this assumption fails remains underexplored. We present Belief-guided Residual Adaptive Control (BRACE), a hierarchical reinforcement learning (RL) framework for reach-avoid navigation under unknown, bounded, spatially varying disturbances. BRACE infers a disturbance belief from model prediction errors and uses that to condition a high-level policy that adapts the reference trajectory. The policy combines a nominal and a belief-guided residual term, trained jointly with a likelihood-ratio advantage reweighting heuristic. We evaluate BRACE in three simulated quadcopter environments with abruptly switching wind fields, and validate it on Crazyflie hardware with fan-generated disturbances. Across these settings, BRACE improves reach-avoid performance over model predictive control and RL baselines.

title: Semantic Synthesis over Brute-Force Search: LLM-Guided Transformation Design for Efficient Learning
author: Usha Shrestha
Radu Timofte
Dmitry Ignatov
abstract: Data transformation pipelines shape the training distribution in computer vision, but designing them is a computationally expensive problem. We investigate whether large language models can enable efficient discovery by synthesizing executable transformation programs outside predefined augmentation spaces. We compare nine strategies under a unified training protocol, including standard augmentation policies, brute-force search, direct code generation with two LLMs, and performance-guided generation using LLMs fine-tuned on accuracy-ordered transformation pairs. When the best candidates are retrained for 20 epochs, LLM-generated transformation programs lead on every dataset, reaching 0.8877 accuracy on CIFAR-10, 0.5825 on CIFAR-100, and 0.9588 on SVHN, surpassing brute-force search over 6,000 candidates. The best transform on CIFAR-10 and SVHN comes from a fine-tuned generator using 270 candidates, while the best on CIFAR-100 comes from an off-the-shelf generator using only 10. This needs 22x fewer candidate evaluations in the generation step and 600x fewer for off-the-shelf generations, relative to brute-force search. Beyond transformation discovery, we analyze the reliability of the reduced-budget evaluation commonly used for augmentation search. Correlating one-epoch selection scores with 20-epoch outcomes reveals strong, weak, and absent predictive relationships depending on the dataset and architecture, with correlations ranging from 0.756 to near zero. A positive control indicates that range restriction alone is unlikely to explain the low correlations. Our results indicate that semantic synthesis with code LLMs provides an efficient alternative to search-based transformation discovery and highlight the importance of validating evaluation fidelity when optimizing data transformations.

title: CoupledFlow: One-Step Neural Operators for Coupled Multi-Physics PDEs
author: Trong Khiem Tran
Minh Long Bui
Phi Le Nguyen
Mrinal Sen
Sanjay Srinivasan
Trong Nghia Hoang
Jana Doppa
abstract: This paper introduces COUPLED FLOW, a new neural operator learning framework for multi-physics PDE systems that captures the co-evolution of multiple physical processes by modeling their cross-process interactions. Unlike existing neural operator methods that primarily target single-physics settings, COUPLED FLOW employs a novel structure-constrained flow matching algorithm to learn process- specific mean velocity fields conditioned on the full multi-physics state. This enables fast and accurate one-step prediction of coupled PDE systems that would otherwise require expensive numerical simulations. A key challenge in training COUPLED FLOW however lies in sampling structure-constrained conditional flow interpolants that capture cross-process correlations and serve as training examples for flow matching. To address this challenge, we derive a multi-physics mean-flow consistency identity that characterizes cross-process interactions and defines the structure-constrained mean-flow matching loss. To provide informative training samples for flow matching with this loss, we develop a principled method for sampling correlated conditional interpolants based on posterior multi-output Gaus- sian processes, which capture richer cross-process correlations than the commonly used endpoint-conditioned linear interpolants. We also establish a theoretical re- sult showing that the Wasserstein-2 distance between the predicted and oracle PDE solution distributions is upper-bounded in terms of the structure-constrained flow matching loss and the smoothness of the learned flow. Experiments across diverse coupled PDE benchmarks demonstrate that COUPLED FLOW consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art neural operators and generative PDE solvers.

title: Explicitly capturing demonstrator multi-modality for distillation into diffusion policies
author: Shao Yuan Chew Chia
Rebecca H. Jiang
Abhinav Agarwal
Andreas Hofmann
Leslie Pack Kaelbling
Russ Tedrake
abstract: The diversity of a distilled diffusion policy's outputs matters beyond how it impacts the policy's success rate. In particular, downstream applications like test-time search and policy improvement require exploration. Thus, we want to distill multi-modal demonstrators into diffusion policies which reproduce their conditional action distributions. Standard data collection for behavior cloning applies a sliding window to demonstration episodes, which pairs unique observation histories with actions. These datasets can be fit by a policy that is either multi-modal, or unimodal with high Lipschitz constant to capture a diversity of actions seen at nearby observation samples. Prior work finds that diffusion policies trained on sparse data learn the latter, memorizing one action per observation. We adapt vine sampling to behavior cloning data collection to resolve this ambiguity: at some states the demonstrator visits, query it $k$ times from exactly the same observation. On a synthetic task, we study how the number of actions per observation, $k$, affects the learned policy, and find that larger $k$ yields a policy that better matches the demonstrator's conditional distribution, including its multi-modality and diversity. On a 2D truck unloading task, vine sampling likewise leads to a policy closer to the demonstrator and substantially improves both best-of-$N$ and expert iteration performance.

title: Hybrid Source Code Change Impact Analysis
author: Katharina Stengg
Christian Macho
Martin Pinzger
abstract: Change impact analysis (CIA) helps developers identify code entities impacted by their initial changes. While several approaches for CIA were proposed, they still struggle with either low precision or low recall, thereby increasing manual effort for developers to verify the results. Furthermore, limitations in the used datasets and experimental setups can bias the results reported by many CIA approaches. In this paper, we first address the dataset limitations by manually labeling 1,931 changed code entities stemming from 263 commits of 22 open-source Java projects. Next, we introduce two variants of katIA, our code change impact analysis approach that combines static impact analysis with the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). The first variant uses a single prompt (katIA-SP) for refining an initial static impact set while the second variant uses three specialized agents (katIA-MA). The evaluation with our curated dataset shows that katIA-SP with Gemini 2.5 Flash achieved an F1-score of 22.4% when matching impacted entities by their fully qualified names (FQN) and 27.0% when matching them by their class and entity names (CE). The latter shows an improvement of 2.0 percentage points over the state-of-the-art. This score is further improved by katIA-MA which, using Gemini 2.5 Flash, yields an FQN-matching F1-score of 29.1% and a CE-matching F1-score of 33.3%. While these improvements come at the cost of increased median generation time from 0.570 s to 11.214 s and median token usage from 1,235 to 6,462 tokens, the improved performance justifies the additional cost. The comparison of three LLMs using katIA-SP finds that Gemini 2.5 Flash is the most consistent model. These results indicate that combining static impact analysis with LLM-based refinement, particularly with the multi-agent variant, can improve code change impact analysis.

title: DMP-Oriented Anisotropic Mesh Adaptation for SUPG Finite Element Methods for Time-Dependent Convection-Diffusion Problems
author: Xianping Li
abstract: We study discrete bound preservation for fully discrete piecewise-linear streamline upwind Petrov--Galerkin (SUPG) finite element approximations of time-dependent convection--diffusion equations on anisotropic triangular meshes. Although the continuous homogeneous-source problem satisfies a parabolic maximum principle, SUPG approximations can exhibit nonphysical undershoots and overshoots. We derive sufficient nodal discrete maximum principle (DMP) conditions that account for the stabilized mass matrix, the combined effects of physical and streamline diffusion, time-step restrictions, and transfer between successive meshes. The analysis identifies a SUPG-effective diffusion tensor and motivates an anisotropic metric aligned with its inverse. We construct a combined metric that retains the effective-tensor geometry while introducing solution-dependent mesh density through recovered Hessian information. The resulting DMP conditions provide a theoretical basis for anisotropic mesh design. Numerical experiments for time-dependent transport problems with isotropic and moderately anisotropic diffusion demonstrate that, under mass-compatible limited SUPG stabilization, the combined metric substantially reduces measured undershoots relative to other methods at matched nominal mesh budgets, although improved bound behavior can carry an accuracy penalty. A controlled tensor--density comparison in the anisotropic transport test supports a contribution from the effective tensor beyond the prescribed mesh density.

title: BAT-WAM: Bridging Action and Touch in World-Action Models for Dexterous Hands
author: Dong Fang
Feixuan Huang
Yuanxin Zhong
Yuxiang Gao
Qi Song
Yunlong Wang
Xiaosong Jia
Yu-Gang Jiang
abstract: Dexterous manipulation with world action models (WAMs) relies on hand configuration and contact information, yet joint-state and whole-hand tactile observations may be partially or entirely missing. RGB images provide scene context and hand-object geometry but are insufficient to reliably recover these missing modalities. We further observe a correlation between hand state and tactile information. Motivated by this observation, we introduce BAT-WAM, a framework that bridges visual, joint-state, and tactile representations for WAMs. BAT-WAM learns separate codebooks and decoders for the tactile and action streams. An RGB-conditioned continuous latent bridge connects the two streams for bidirectional learning, while visual information serves as continuous context. Under the HTBench evaluation protocol, BAT-WAM reduces the root mean squared error (RMSE) of tactile reconstruction by 34.73% under fully masked conditions and 38.84% under partially masked conditions, relative to an image-conditioned HandTouch checkpoint. For future tactile prediction conditioned on target-time RGB and historical actions, it reduces mean RMSE by 85.56% relative to OpenWAM with HandTouch. Real-robot experiments further show that BAT-WAM consistently outperforms related WAM baselines in dexterous manipulation. Generalization experiments on unseen objects and scenes also demonstrate substantial improvements over baseline models. These findings support joint modeling of visual context, hand state, and touch as a representation approach for multimodal WAMs.

title: When Safety Becomes An Outlier: Understanding the Retention of LLM Safety Behaviors
author: Binchi Zhang
Hadi Abdullah
Yiwei Cai
Jundong Li
abstract: Safety-aligned large language models often lose their safety behaviors after fine-tuning, even when safety data are included. While this fragility is well documented, its underlying cause remains unclear. In this paper, we propose that formulaic refusal strings can function as outlier modes: narrow, weakly grounded response patterns that are easy to fit but vulnerable to subsequent updates. Controlled experiments support this account: fixed refusals are acquired much like arbitrary constant strings, in contrast to prompt-grounded natural responses. Motivated by these findings, we introduce Naturalness-Enhanced Safety Targets (NEST), a safety alignment framework that improves safety retention by constructing natural, context-aware safety targets that keep safety responses within the model's existing output distribution and grounded in semantics. We instantiate NEST in both supervised and preference-based alignment settings, using perplexity under the original model as a proxy for distributional support. Across multiple models and alignment regimes, natural safety targets improve both immediate safety and its retention under continued fine-tuning without sacrificing helpfulness. These findings suggest a practical principle for more durable safety alignment: construct safety targets that draw on the model's existing language capabilities and remain grounded in the meaning of each request.

title: SWEET: Mitigating Spurious Feature Reliance in LLM Reasoning via Weight Editing
author: Zhizhang Fu
Lucas Zhao
Michalis Korakakis
Mengru Ding
Lukasz Szpruch
Yue Zhang
abstract: Reasoning in large language models can be disrupted by simple input perturbations (e.g. adding irrelevant distractors), suggesting reliance on spurious correlations. Identifying and suppressing the spurious features involved in long chain-of-thought reasoning remains challenging. We introduce Spurious-feature WEight EdiTing (SWEET), a training-free method that combines counterfactual interventions with mechanistic interpretability to identify and suppress spurious-features. SWEET extracts token- and sequence-level behavioral directions from activation contrasts between original problems and their counterfactual variants - capturing local and global patterns of spurious reasoning. It then localizes the responsible MLP neurons and attention heads and suppresses their contributions along these directions through weight edits. Using only 20 original-counterfactual pairs for direction extraction, SWEET improves accuracy by an average of 11.8 percentage points on perturbed inputs and 2 points on original inputs across five open-weight reasoning models and five reasoning benchmarks. It also reduces the relative gap between original and perturbed accuracies from 17.6% to 2.5%. Analyses identify two recurring forms of spurious reasoning, i.e. over-integrating irrelevant conditions and overthinking, and provide mechanistic evidence that SWEET improves reasoning robustness by suppressing both behavioral directions.

title: DM-Call: Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling with Cumulative Verification Feedback
author: Minhyeong Yu
Wonduk Seo
Seunghyun Lee
abstract: Reliable function calling requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to select appropriate functions and generate arguments consistent with user intent. However, syntactically valid calls may still be semantically incorrect due to inappropriate function selection or mismatched arguments. In this paper, we propose Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling (DM-Call), a framework that combines local schema validation with separate decision-model verification of function selection and argument correctness. For rejected candidates, DM-Call accumulates verification probabilities, binary judgments, and schema errors across attempts. A hybrid feedback representation further combines numerical probabilities with verbal correctness labels to guide iterative refinement without executing external tools. Extensive evaluation across BFCL and API-Bank (first-call) demonstrates DM-Call boosts function-calling accuracy versus direct generation, at modest additional cost.

title: An Analysis of Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation
author: Francisco S. Melo
Sean P. Meyn
M. Isabel Ribeiro
abstract: We address the problem of computing the optimal Q-function in Markov decision problems with infinite state-space. We analyze the convergence properties of several variations of Q-learning when combined with function approximation, extending the analysis of TD-learning in Tsitsiklis and Van Roy (1996) to stochastic control settings. We identify conditions under which such approximate methods converge with probability 1. We conclude with a brief discussion on the general applicability of our results and compare them with several related works.

title: Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning
author: Haoran Xu
Pragya Srivastava
Xinjie Liu
Siddhant Agarwal
Amy Zhang
abstract: Learning accurate off-policy state-action value functions (Q-functions) from offline datasets becomes harder as the task horizon grows. One-step temporal-difference (TD) learning bootstraps after every transition, so small per-step errors accumulate along the horizon, and early states can be badly misvalued even when the TD loss is small. Multi-step TD shortens this chain by following the dataset trajectory for several steps; however, since the behavior policy is often suboptimal, every followed action adds a bias, and no fixed number of steps suits a whole trajectory. In this paper, we propose Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), a simple method that enables accurate long-horizon value learning by automatically balancing between one-step and multi-step returns. HQL extends a target through a dataset action only when the critic values it at least as highly as the best-of-N actions sampled from the BC policy, and otherwise falls back to a one-step target. We show that this rule is a principled off-policy correction that needs no action densities, which makes HQL compatible with expressive flow and diffusion policies. Experiments show that HQL avoids the failures of both one-step and multi-step TD on a combination-lock task across horizons, and outperforms prior horizon-reduction methods on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks.

title: DPDP: Diffusion Policy-Steered Diffusion Planner for Offline Reinforcement Learning
author: Ruyi An
Mingyuan Zhou
abstract: In offline reinforcement learning, diffusion models fill two roles with complementary strengths. Typically guided by a critic, a diffusion policy is value-aware and favors high-return, behavior-supported actions, but it is short-sighted: it never lays out the states it intends to visit. A diffusion planner is far-sighted, synthesizing such a long-horizon trajectory, but it is only behavior-driven at execution, realizing each planned transition using only offline http://behavior.Each is strong exactly where the other is weak. We introduce DPDP to bring them together at the planner's execution step, where a planned transition becomes an action. Reading the planner's inverse-dynamics executor as a posterior over actions: the environment's transition likelihood relates an action to the planned next state, while the behavioral prior determines its weight under the offline data. Replacing this prior with a value-optimized diffusion policy preserves the planned transition likelihood and favors valuable actions that can serve the plan. We target the resulting clean-action distribution in two ways. A training-free sampler composes policy and inverse-dynamics scores at matched action noise levels and applies Langevin correction; this route uses a shared action noise schedule and an approximately common terminal prior. A preference objective instead amortizes the transfer into a single diffusion executor. Across D4RL, DPDP improves the planner it builds on, staying competitive with reactive diffusion policies on locomotion and leading on long-horizon navigation.

title: RoboMoCap: A Large-Scale Whole-Body Motion Capture Dataset with Egocentric Vision for Robot Learning
author: Mayur Deshmukh
Aaron Tung
Junyi Li
Nikash Bhardwaj
Ademi Adeniji
Vincent Liu
Michael Cho
Jiafei Duan
abstract: Humanoid robots must coordinate locomotion and manipulation to navigate complex environments and perform everyday tasks. Learning such behaviours from human demonstrations requires accurate whole-body motion paired with egocentric vision, particularly for lower-body movements and foot placements that are frequently invisible from a first-person perspective. However, existing egocentric datasets often lack high-fidelity optical motion capture or systematic coverage of diverse loco-manipulation behaviours. To address this gap, we introduce RoboMoCap, a large-scale multimodal dataset combining egocentric vision with marker-based optical motion capture, specifically designed for locomotion-centric humanoid learning. RoboMoCap comprises over 200 hours of recordings from 14 participants, featuring six head-mounted cameras, wrist-mounted visual and inertial sensing, and optical full-body motion capture at 120 Hz. The dataset systematically covers diverse locomotion primitives, dynamic whole-body movements, and loco-manipulation tasks, including variable-speed walking, turning, constrained navigation, terrain traversal, object transportation, and manipulation during locomotion. It provides temporally aligned multimodal observations and metric whole-body motion representations, enabling the study of human movement beyond directly observable body regions. We systematically evaluate existing methods on three benchmark tasks: egocentric full-body motion reconstruction, foot contact and placement estimation, and human-to-humanoid motion retargeting. By pairing egocentric vision with high-fidelity human motion across diverse locomotion and interaction scenarios, RoboMoCap provides a foundation for egocentric motion understanding and humanoid learning from human demonstrations.

title: Differentiable Agent-Based Modeling for Multi-Echelon Supply Chains: Gradient-Based Optimization of Heterogeneous Policies at Scale
author: Bulent Soykan
Murtadha Alsayegh
Sean Mondesire
Ghaith Rabadi
abstract: Global supply chains rely on the interactions of thousands of heterogeneous agents, posing significant challenges for optimization. While traditional optimization often assumes homogeneity to ensure tractability, Reinforcement Learning struggles with sample inefficiency when scaling to high-dimensional state spaces. We propose a Differentiable Agent-Based Model for multi-echelon inventory management. By implementing stochastic dynamics via differentiable tensor operations, we enable direct gradient propagation through the simulation. We validate the framework by recovering theoretical Newsvendor optima without supervision. Crucially, we demonstrate ``Mass Personalization'' by optimizing 10,000 distinct agent policies simultaneously in seconds, achieving a 53% cost reduction compared to scalar baselines. Furthermore, we utilize gradient sensitivity analysis to generate causal heatmaps, accurately recovering inherent lead-time delays from the computation graph. This approach bridges the gap between simulation and optimization, enabling the efficient training of self-correcting Digital Twins.

title: GradReason: LLMs as Meta-Learners that Replace Training Epochs with Training-Data-Free Weight Updates
author: Ali Mohammadi Ruzbahani
Abbas Yazdinejad
Hadis Karimipour
abstract: Standard training recipes make a fixed number of passes over the training data, even when an epoch mostly adds mini-batch noise. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that reads the weight and gradient history of a run can replace some of these epochs with updates that compute no gradient and read no training image. In GradReason, an LLM agent is called every ten epochs. In a restricted sandbox, it analyses recent weight snapshots, epoch-mean gradients, and validation metrics, then submits a Python program that computes new weights and a plan marking each of the next ten epochs as data or virtual. A virtual epoch is kept only if it passes a forward-only check on 5,000 held-out validation images. In 120 runs on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with three architectures, Claude Opus 5.5 used 32.8% fewer data epochs than the 80-epoch recipe at 0.31 percentage points lower test accuracy (95% CI -0.72 to +0.09; 0.94 points on ResNet-18), on the recipe's own frontier of data against accuracy. Unprompted, Opus averaged recent weight snapshots in every run. This choice produced the savings: a fixed rule with the same acceptance check but extrapolations from prior work saved 5.4% of the data epochs, and the same rule with averaging added saved 25.0%. The LLM's contribution is to find a working update within a single run; once found, a fixed rule implements it equally well. An Opus run cost 0.68 USD, but at this scale the agent's latency exceeded the GPU time it saved.

title: Efficient 3D plant segmentation through multiscale graph learning and optimized geometric processing
author: Jesus Ivan Ruiz-Martinez
Andres Mendez-Vazquez
Eduardo Rodriguez-Tello
abstract: Plant organ segmentation on compact computing platforms requires accurate predictions and affordable geometric preparation. We develop and evaluate a multiscale edge based graph attention model that combines local shape descriptors, two neighborhood scales and a residual stem and leaf correction in approximately 78 thousand parameters. The engineering application is plant point cloud segmentation for precision agriculture, assessed through grouped accuracy experiments and physical Raspberry Pi 5 inference. Broad comparisons with hierarchical, graph and transformer baselines establish PointNeXt as the strongest external accuracy reference among the tested local recipes. A nested four variant ablation on a local maize collection separates geometric information from the combined multiscale configuration across seven outer groups and three seeds. The complete model achieves the highest mean intersection over union, 86.36%, although uncertainty and boundary errors qualify the contribution of each component. We then optimize full cloud principal component analysis, sampling and neighbor queries without changing learned weights or descriptor definitions. All 1,180 paired desktop comparisons on PlantNet and TomatoWUR preserve exact logits and predictions. Multiscale pipeline latency falls from 330.33 to 96.82 milliseconds on PlantNet and from 1,054.52 to 463.10 milliseconds on TomatoWUR. PointNeXt also benefits from optimized sampling and remains faster over the complete pipeline. These results support compact graph learning with reduced geometric overhead, while physical board measurements establish inference feasibility rather than energy efficiency or readiness for autonomous flight.

title: RoutingTrie: Metadata Routing for Constrained Generative Retrieval
author: Darshan Fofadiya
Yang Liu
Shuying Sun
Kyumin Park
Juhana Kangaspunta
abstract: Advances in large language models and semantic IDs (SIDs) have brought generative retrieval (GR) into industrial applications. These systems must return items that satisfy request metadata constraints as well as relevance requirements. A catalog trie ensures SID validity, but filtering metadata only after generation wastes computation on rejected candidates and may leave too few eligible results. We propose RoutingTrie to incorporate metadata constraints before beam selection. RoutingTrie maintains one shared SID trie and builds a compact index for each metadata field using Dense Bitset or Sparse List. We derive a storage cost formula to guide the choice between these index representations for different field distributions. During decoding, field probes determine whether requested values occur below candidate edges and produce a combined mask that guides beam selection. Experiments on ShopTrie, our configurable synthetic benchmark, demonstrate compact storage and efficient CPU and GPU probing across diverse metadata distributions. In a production replay, RoutingTrie raises Hit@100 from 67.5\% to 96.1\%, a gain of 28.6 percentage points, with only 1.1 ms latency increase. We will release the ShopTrie generator, benchmark scripts, and RoutingTrie CPU and Triton GPU implementations to support reproducibility.

title: Where Should Models Run? A Collaborative Inference Framework for Embodied Intelligence in 6G
author: Wanlu Sun
Zhenhui Yuan
Xiang Ji
Yi Han
Qing Li
Gan Zheng
abstract: Embodied intelligence systems rely on fast and reliable inference to enable real-time perception, reasoning, and control. Recent advances in large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) models, including Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, have significantly enhanced the capabilities of embodied agents in complex environments. However, deploying these models remains challenging due to the limited computational resources and energy budgets of robotic platforms. A fundamental question is where inference should be executed. Collaborative inference, which partitions models across end devices, edge servers, and the cloud, has emerged as a promising solution. Yet determining the optimal partitioning point remains an open problem, as it depends on wireless network conditions, model structure, and privacy requirements. This article reviews the state of the art in collaborative inference for embodied intelligence and proposes an edge-centric framework in which the edge coordinates model partitioning and execution. Through both simulation and real-world experiments over WiFi and 5G networks, we demonstrate that the optimal partitioning strategy varies with network conditions and model structure. We further identify latency-minimizing partition points for ResNet-101, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and OpenVLA-7B in collaborative inference between NVIDIA Jetson Nano or AGX Xavier devices and an AGX Thor edge server under varying wireless conditions. Finally, we discuss the future directions for collaborative inference in 6G-empowered embodied intelligence systems.

title: Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping for Token-Efficient LLM Reasoning
author: Zhe Chen
Xiaolin Zhou
Xiyang Hu
abstract: Extended reasoning can help language models solve complex problems, but long responses often contain both useful computations and redundant checks. Conventional length penalties encourage shorter responses without distinguishing the functions of intermediate steps. We propose Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping (PCRS), a framework that combines phase identification with training-time reward allocation. We investigate two classification routes: PCRS-H with a hidden-state classifier and PCRS-T with a frozen text classifier. Our main text classifier implementation assigns overlapping reasoning, execution, and revision labels to native chunks, then uses these labels and exact repetition to adjust existing token penalties. We compare the completed configurations on six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks and examine four reward-weight settings with the text classifier. Compared with a baseline using token-level length penalties, the default text classifier configuration reduces mean response length by 3.13%; sampled Pass@1 is approximately 62.07% for both methods, while oracle Pass@16 rises from 86.08% to 87.67%. These results show how phase-informed penalty allocation can reduce output volume and improve multi-attempt coverage without inference-time classification.

title: MoTo: Mixture of Tokenizers Towards Fair Multilingual Language Modeling
author: GÃ¼l Sena AltÄ±ntaÅ
Colin Raffel
abstract: Large language models rely on a single tokenizer that is chosen at training time and fixed thereafter. Most tokenizers are trained on English-dominant corpora, making them under-serve morphologically rich and non-Latin-script languages, where they can produce fragmented representations, longer sequence lengths, and reduced information density during training. We propose Mixture of Tokenizers MoTo, a modular tokenization framework that trains dedicated per-language BPE tokenizers and composes them into a unified superset vocabulary, where tokens shared across languages are deduplicated into a common ID space. Each tokenizer maintains its own normalization policy, pre-tokenization rules, and vocabulary budget. Despite allocating significantly fewer entries to English, MoTo retains English performance while delivering consistent gains across 18 out of 21 typologically diverse languages spanning six scripts, with improvements most pronounced on morphologically complex and non-Latin-script languages that are systematically underserved by English-dominant tokenizer design. Our results suggest that modular subword tokenization is a practical and extensible alternative to monolithic tokenization for multilingual parity.

title: Building and Auditing Chemical Datasets with LLMs: A General LLM-as-a-Judge Framework Applied to Homogeneous Catalytic PET Depolymerisation
author: Muhammad bin Javaid
Karim K. Ben Hicham
Enkhnyam Battulga
Alexander Mitsos
Martin Grohe
abstract: Large language models can rapidly extract structured multivariate experimental data from the chemistry literature, yet verifying thousands of generated records without ground truth remains difficult. We present a general, citation-grounded extraction and verification methodology centered on an independent "LLM-as-a-judge", applied to the literature on homogeneous catalytic poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) depolymerisation. In this pipeline, an extractor LLM generates schema-enforced records from research papers with citations to document chunks tagged with universally unique identifiers (UUIDs); an independent LLM judge then reads the full paper alongside each record, flags unsupported fields, and proposes cited corrections. Prompt ablations show that requiring chunk-level citations not only provides provenance down to specific paragraphs and tables but also improves extraction accuracy. Before deploying the judge at scale, we benchmarked it against manual evaluation on extractions from a hand-curated reference set of 295 ionic-liquid-catalysed PET glycolysis experiments. The judge agreed with human evaluation on 85.7% of reviewed records and was significantly more effective than a heuristic string-matching baseline at catching errors across related experiments. Deployed across 3,942 extracted records from 561 papers, the framework accepted 67.5% of them as written. Its proposed corrections concentrated on quantitative fields, where the extractor often conflated related experiments. We release the extracted dataset with the complete LLM judge audit logs, as well as the Chemistry Data Extractor Toolkit, an open-source application implementing this end-to-end pipeline in a code-free, browser-based environment for document parsing, customizable schema and prompt design, model-agnostic extraction and auditing, interactive provenance-highlighted review, and reproducible dataset bundling.

title: When Is High-Bandwidth Flash Cost-Effective for LLM Inference?
author: Zhiyu An
Yiping Li
Wan Du
abstract: Can high-bandwidth flash (HBF) make LLM inference cheaper than adding GPUs? By storing weights closer to the GPU than SSD, HBF may reduce the number of GPUs needed for model capacity. However, this integration is only justified if it meets service targets and its cost is recovered. We simulate this integration using public component data across nine dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, five workloads, two GPU platforms, and 1--100 GPUs. At fixed demand, HBF reduces the minimum GPU count to meet a service target in 98 of 468 comparisons; majority of them are paused and short sessions, 63 remain cost-effective at half a GPU price per HBF stack. For single short-chat users, HBF enables large MoEs, e.g. DeepSeek V3 and Kimi K2, to meet a relaxed service target on one RTX~4090 GPU, where conventional serving fails. At fixed GPU count, HBF improves throughput in 48\% of matched comparisons below 16 GPUs and 13\% at larger counts. Even at 100 RTX~4090-scale GPUs, cascaded HBF raises offline throughput by 16.4--26.5$\times$ for three large MoEs. We found savings and throughput gains arise in different scenarios.

title: Agents Propose, Code Verifies, Humans Decide: Verified Agentic Ingestion of Heterogeneous Scientific Tables into Relational Databases
author: Bharatha Rankothge
Suzanne Hodgkins
Virginia Rich
Michael Kirby
abstract: Public scientific datasets rarely arrive analysis-ready. They arrive as messy folders of wide matrices, long tables, spreadsheets, and per-cohort files whose keys and encodings differ, and every reanalysis must reconnect them first. A coding agent can automate this, but its mistakes can look plausible, and without an audit trail, a mistake that corrupts data can go uncaught.
